text:
IBIA shipboard biofuel blend checklist annexed to MEPC 85/INF.10

Aimed at operators bunkering and burning FAME blends for the first time

Based on CIMAC guideline 04|2024 on marine fuels containing FAME

Part of the update to the IBIA/BIMCO Shipmaster's Bunkering Manual

Bunker industry body IBIA's shipboard biofuel blend checklist for FAME-based fuels has been issued by the IMO as an annex to document MEPC 85/INF.10, putting the guidance in front of member states ahead of the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) session that runs from November 30 to December 3.

The checklist was developed by the IBIA Technical Working Group as part of the ongoing update of the IBIA/BIMCO Shipmaster's Bunkering Manual, and is intended to help vessel operators with the practical side of bunkering and consuming biofuel blends, particularly for the first time, IBIA said in a statement.

In the submission, dated September 3, IBIA notes that the increased use of biofuel blends brings the potential for different and additional operational risks for the ship, especially for operators planning to bunker and consume blends for the first time.

These risks can be addressed through robust fuel management both before delivery and once onboard, IBIA says.

The checklist is based on the International Council on Combustion Engines (CIMAC) guideline 04|2024, Marine fuels containing FAME, and IBIA says operators looking at bio-based products other than FAME blends should seek guidance from the engine maker and the ship's recognised organisation instead.

Among the practical points, the checklist calls for bunker tanks to be stripped before a blend is first loaded, warns that blends may loosen accumulated deposits in tanks and fuel systems and increase filter loading in the early period of use, and suggests retesting fuel quality if a blend has been stored for more than six months.

It also asks crews to check the blend ratio and sustainability documentation alongside the bunker delivery note before accepting the fuel, and to allow for the lower energy content of blends in voyage fuel planning.

As Ship & Bunker reported last month, the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) has warned that blend ratios, such as B24 or B30, are typically supplier-declared rather than independently verified.

The guidance arrives at a time when biofuel has cemented its place as part of the current marine fuel mix, but there are signs that recent demand has failed to match earlier enthusiasm.

Blend sales at Singapore, the largest bunkering hub, totalled 519,820 mt over the first eight months of 2026, half the 1.04 million mt sold in the same period last year, according to data from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) reported by Ship & Bunker.

name: International Maritime Organization
title: Study Tests Regulatory Applicability of Continuous Emissions Measurement
description:
With the battle lines forming for the International Maritime Organization to finalize and adopt its Net Zero Framework, a new study is looking at the validity of continuous emissions measurement technology as it applies to the regulation.
They are looking at the use of real-time monitoring aboard LNG vessels versus the current modeling used in assessing emissions.
The initiative will see LR acting as the independent verifier, working with Seapeak, Kongsberg Maritime and Tunable to advance emissions compliance through the deployment and verification of onboard emissions monitoring technology.
The project will evaluate measured emissions data from a newly built LNG carrier scheduled for delivery in early 2027, with monitoring and data analysis continuing throughout the year.
It will measure the accuracy of Kongsberg Maritime’s Continuous Emissions Monitoring System (CEMS), which incorporates Tunable’s gas analysis technology, on board a new LNG carrier.
text:
With the battle lines forming for the International Maritime Organization to finalize and adopt its Net Zero Framework, a new study is looking at the validity of continuous emissions measurement technology as it applies to the regulation. They are looking at the use of real-time monitoring aboard LNG vessels versus the current modeling used in assessing emissions.

The IMO adopted in 2023 its Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) and the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rating scheme as the first step to cut carbon intensity. The MEPC is set to hold its next session starting at the end of November in an attempt to complete a draft, followed potentially by the next Extraordinary Session to put the Net Zero Framework to a vote for members.

“The industry currently relies on default emissions factors and test bed data to estimate environmental performance,” explains Panos Mitrou, SVP Shipping Strategy for Lloyd's Register. “This initiative enables industry stakeholders the opportunity to compare estimated emissions performance against direct measurements from a vessel operating in real-world conditions. The results will generate valuable insights into the role continuous emissions monitoring can play in supporting more accurate reporting as well as an improved operational understanding that can support emissions minimization.”

The new joint development project will bring together expertise from across the maritime value chain to provide independent evidence on the accuracy and reliability of continuous emissions monitoring technologies for LNG-fuelled vessels. The initiative will see LR acting as the independent verifier, working with Seapeak, Kongsberg Maritime and Tunable to advance emissions compliance through the deployment and verification of onboard emissions monitoring technology.

text:
Since the current conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February, the International Maritime Organization, IMO, has verified 80 attacks on international shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

This has resulted in the deaths of at least 22 seafarers and injuries to many others.

In the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, dozens of fatalities have reportedly resulted from attacks on international shipping in recent months, although precise numbers are difficult to verify.

Attacks in the Red Sea have also resumed, with four fatalities confirmed in the latest attack by the Houthis on a merchant vessel on 11 August, the UN agency said.

Here’s Roel Hoenders, Chief of Staff at IMO:

“Apart from putting seafarers’ lives at risk, attacks on merchant shipping are having a severe impact on global supply chains and people everywhere around the world. - And let’s not forget that 22 crew have already been killed since the conflict in the Middle East began on 28 February.”

Mr. Dominguez stressed that in the Strait of Hormuz, the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, “it is not only one country attacking merchant vessels”.

UN rights chief warns democracy has almost disappeared in Nicaragua

Democracy in Nicaragua is being dismantled at an alarming pace, the UN human rights chief warned on Wednesday, as a new report detailed growing political repression, arbitrary arrests and the silencing of critics.

Presenting the findings, Volker Türk said power is becoming increasingly concentrated in the hands of the executive and the ruling party.

“The report traces the near-total capture of State institutions by the ruling party,” he said, describing a pattern of “systematic abuse of power” that has eroded checks and balances and left many people without protection when their rights are violated.

“The situation is utterly indefensible,” he added.

Basic rights dismantled

The report covers the period from June 2025 to June 2026 and paints a picture of a country where independent political activity has almost disappeared. It warns that proposed constitutional changes could block organized opposition groups from future elections and extend presidential terms to as long as seven years.

According to the report, the authorities also continue to use arbitrary detention as a tool against dissent. At least 46 people were reportedly still being held at the end of the reporting period, while UN investigators documented ongoing cases of enforced disappearance and deaths in custody.

Mr. Türk called on the Government to immediately free anyone detained without legal grounds.

The report also highlights a sustained crackdown on civil society and the media. More than 5,500 organizations have been dissolved over the past eight years, and at least 56 media outlets have been shut down.

“There is almost nothing left to shut down,” the High Commissioner said.

He urged Nicaragua’s authorities to reverse course and re-engage with regional and international human rights bodies.

AI’s role in ‘denialism’ trend must be stopped, says rights expert

The Human Rights Council has called on governments everywhere to counter the growing trend of so-called “denialism” politics, which often features the non-acceptance of genocide and other crimes against humanity.

Speaking at the council in Geneva, independent human rights expert, Bernard Duhaime, noted a recent wave of denialist statements by government officials, politicians and other actors worldwide.

Rapporteurs and other independent experts appointed by the council are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work.

Countries must actively counter any efforts to glorify those responsible for crimes against humanity, particularly considering the rise of social media and AI systems which amplify denialism, Mr. Duhaime insisted:

“We live at a dangerous time where ideologues and warmongers seek to fuel polarisation, hatred and chaos for their own political gains. It is high time to remind them of our collective commitment to human rights, accountability, and the rule of law.”

Mr. Duhaime, who works in an independent capacity, is tasked by the Human Rights Council to promote truth, justice, reparations and non-recurrence of crimes.

Delivering his report to the Council’s 47 Member States, he called on all countries to be vigilant about “politicians and corporate actors who seek to weaponize freedom of expression” and “manipulate history for political or other ideological ends”, while also inciting violence and silencing dissenting voices.

“Denialism” is increasingly used to undermine justice for vulnerable populations by spreading divisive narratives, Mr. Duhaime said, explaining that the trend risks eroding democratic institutions and accountability by replacing the truth with “emotionally-charged narratives”.

And although government oversight is key to combating supporters of denialism, the independent rights expert warned that “in too many cases” national legislation has become “tools of restriction and denial”.

“Combating denialism must never serve as a pretext for censorship or repression,” Mr. Duhaime told the Council.

text:
The United States has launched a new strategy to expand international demand for American biofuels, signaling that overseas markets will play a growing role in the sector's future.

Announced by US Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins at the 17th annual Growth Energy Biofuels Summit, the American Biofuels Trade Outlook centers on four priorities: increasing on-road ethanol blending, removing foreign restrictions on US biofuels, targeting high-impact markets, and shaping international aviation and maritime regulations.

The strategy arrives as US ethanol exports reached record levels. The country exported 2.18 billion gallons in 2025, up 13% from the previous record in 2024. Exports represented 13.3% of US production, making international demand an increasingly critical part of the market balance.

Despite these positive trends, further growth is not guaranteed. Many prospective markets protect domestic producers, restrict crop-based fuels, or lack the infrastructure needed to turn blending targets into consumption. The new outlook recognizes that biofuels' global role will depend as much on market access and regulatory treatment as on production and price.

What Are the Four Pillars of the American Biofuels Trade Outlook?

1. Increase On-Road Ethanol Blending

The first pillar combines two objectives: encouraging E10 adoption in new markets and stabilizing access to countries that already have E10 policies.

The USDA sees potential breakthrough markets in Latin America and growth opportunities in Southeast Asia. E10 offers an accessible route to significant new demand because it can generally be used in vehicles without the specialized equipment required for higher ethanol blends. It can also help importing countries in several ways:

Diversify fuel supplies

Reduce petroleum dependence

Meet octane requirements

At the same time, the USDA plans to address policy implementation challenges across approximately 20 existing E10 markets. Announced blending targets do not always translate into physical demand. Infrastructure gaps, inconsistent standards, delayed mandates, and difficult import procedures can all limit consumption.

This pillar seeks both expansion and stability: opening new markets while ensuring that established blending policies create reliable demand.

2. Remove Foreign Restrictions

The second pillar aims to challenge foreign policies that limit the use of US crop-based biofuels. The European Union is a particular focus because its treatment of crop-based fuels can restrict their contribution to transport decarbonization targets.

These rules matter beyond conventional road fuels. Restrictions tied to feedstocks or lifecycle greenhouse gas calculations can also affect whether US-produced fuels qualify for use in aviation and marine markets.

For the US, removing such barriers could broaden the range of applications available to corn- and soybean-based fuels. But this will require more than conventional trade promotion.

Many restrictions are embedded in climate and sustainability policy. Accordingly, US exporters must demonstrate both environmental performance and commercial competitiveness.

3. Target High-Impact Markets

The third pillar will deploy USDA market-access programs and the America First Trade Promotion Program to pursue strategic growth. India was highlighted as a potential market for on-road expansion, alongside Indonesia, Japan, and Vietnam.

The USDA is seeking access to a distinct and politically sensitive part of the Indian market. The same tension may emerge elsewhere: countries can value ethanol's energy-security benefits while using blending mandates to support domestic farmers and producers.

Federal trade programs may help build commercial relationships and address technical barriers. However, the largest gains will depend on whether target countries change policies that favor local supply.

4. Shape Global Regulations

The fourth pillar calls for greater US engagement with the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Maritime Organization. The objective is to secure fair treatment for US biofuels as global aviation and shipping regulations evolve.

These sectors could become significant sources of low-carbon fuel demand because both are difficult to electrify. Access will depend on how international frameworks calculate lifecycle emissions, recognize different production pathways, and treat crop-based feedstocks.

More Insights on Aviation and Marine

Sustainable Aviation Fuel Monthly Snapshot

Bio-Bunkering at a Glance: Marine Biofuels Monthly Update

Lower-carbon farming practices, renewable process energy, and carbon capture could improve the position of US fuels. Their value in international markets, however, will depend on whether regulatory frameworks recognize those emissions reductions.

What Does the Strategy Mean for Biofuel Markets?

For US producers, the outlook confirms that exports are becoming structurally important. Domestic gasoline demand may offer limited long-term growth as vehicle efficiency improves and electrification advances. International blending programs provide another outlet for producers and, indirectly, for US corn and soybean growers.

Additionally, current economic strains between Iran and the US have placed added pressure on domestic fuel markets, driving average fuel costs to record levels. These considerations have made the calls for alternative fuel sources, including biofuels, a much larger part of the conversation.

Globally, the strategy reflects biofuels’ evolution from primarily domestic policy tools into more widely traded energy commodities. Yet the market will not become fully open. Governments will continue to balance competitively priced imports against domestic agricultural, energy-security, and industrial priorities.

Competition will increasingly extend beyond price. Market share will also depend on verified carbon intensity, reliable supply, and compatibility with national and international rules. The outlook's emphasis on both trade barriers and global regulation reflects that shift.

Market Access Will Determine the Outcome

The American Biofuels Trade Outlook identifies four credible routes to growth. But its commercial effect will depend on measurable policy changes and physical trade.

The outlook serves as an important statement of intent, not a guarantee of demand. Its progress will show whether the US can convert record exports into a broader and more durable role for American biofuels in global energy markets.

title: Oman: Advancing sustainable fuels for aviation and maritime industry | ZAWYA
description:
Global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production is expected to reach roughly 2.4 million tonnes this year - less than one percent of all aviation fuel consumed.
The maritime industry, meanwhile, is pursuing wind-assist technologies, efficiency improvements, and dual-fuel vessels, but its transition to sustainable fuels remains problematic.
Behind the crunch lie two linked constraints: limited availability of sustainable feedstocks and biocrudes suitable for refining, and insufficient biorefinery capacity.
Its cultivation can generate biocrude suitable for conversion into high-quality sustainable fuel, alongside biomass that can be used for other productive purposes.
The country stands to benefit substantially from switching to sustainable fuels, particularly as new technologies move towards full cost competitiveness.
text:
Nearly all fuel used today derives from fossil fuels. In reality, for hard-to-abate sectors like aviation, shipping and heavy road transport, there is limited availability of viable sustainable fuel available at the scale required to undertake a meaningful shift. The small pool of biofuel drawing on used cooking oil and tallow is expensive, variable in quality and difficult to access. Unlike passenger and lightweight vehicles - which can take advantage of advancing battery technology - aircraft and vessels carrying heavy payloads across oceans cannot, and will continue to require the energy density that liquid fuels provide.

The constraint at hand carries severe consequences. Global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production is expected to reach roughly 2.4 million tonnes this year - less than one percent of all aviation fuel consumed. The maritime industry, meanwhile, is pursuing wind-assist technologies, efficiency improvements, and dual-fuel vessels, but its transition to sustainable fuels remains problematic. Reaching net-zero by 2050 will require annual SAF output in the vicinity of 500 million tonnes - a more than 200-fold expansion within 24 years. Behind the crunch lie two linked constraints: limited availability of sustainable feedstocks and biocrudes suitable for refining, and insufficient biorefinery capacity. Refiners are, understandably, reluctant to commit capital without assurance of consistent feedstock supply.

While bio-based fuels already exist, their supply base is limited and, in certain respects, contentious. Crop-derived feedstocks - including corn, soy and palm - compete directly with food production and can drive land conversion, including the expansion of large-scale monocultures at the expense of natural ecosystems and, in some cases, primary forest. Used cooking oil and animal tallow belong to the more defensible alternatives, but their available supply is inherently limited and increasingly sought after. The dominant SAF production pathway today relies heavily on these and other lipid feedstocks, making diversification increasingly important. Under EU regulation, this constraint is reflected in policy: waste oils and fats sit in Annex IX, Part B of the Renewable Energy Directive and are capped at 1.7% of the transport fuel mix. Advanced feedstocks such as forestry residues, other lignocellulosic materials and algae can mitigate many of these pressures.

With freshwater already scarce and limited national land suitable for agriculture, balancing food security, energy security, and decarbonisation poses a formidable challenge for countries like Oman. Absent a domestic feedstock, Oman's alternative is longer term reliance on imported fuel, or imported feedstock for domestic refining.

Oman does possess, however, several thousand kilometres of pristine coastline, among the highest levels of solar irradiance globally, and extensive desert land with no competing agricultural value. These conditions offer a strong match for a newly identified marine microalga – Sphaerica - a feedstock with potentially high commercial as well as environmental value. Its cultivation can generate biocrude suitable for conversion into high-quality sustainable fuel, alongside biomass that can be used for other productive purposes.

This particular organism needs no freshwater but thrives in very high salinity seawater, and the water drawn into the system can be recycled through multiple cycles rather than extracted once and then discarded - a meaningful distinction for a country that already directs much of its scarce freshwater to agriculture.

Nor does it require arable soil. Cultivation takes place on land with no food-producing value, leaving soil health undisturbed, within an enclosed photobioreactor system designed not to degrade the land beneath it and using lightweight, modular construction. Genuine diversification means directing future investment towards feedstocks that can grow at scale and achieve acceptable cost structures without reproducing the sustainability problems associated with earlier generations of biofuels. Oman's coastline and sunlight give it the means to lead that shift.

I’m presently visiting the country, leading a delegation from a UK biotechnology company, HutanBio, which is dedicated to innovation in this respect. Taking part in the Oman Climate Week we benefit from conversation with multiple parties, exploring ways our bioenergy platform can be taken forward in Oman, thereby scaling production of a sustainable, quality bio/fuel, to serve Oman as well as international markets.

Oman – along with the wider region – continues to evolve as a vibrant hub for air passengers, air cargo, and maritime transport. The country stands to benefit substantially from switching to sustainable fuels, particularly as new technologies move towards full cost competitiveness. By pushing ahead with the bio-energy opportunities now taking shape, Oman has an opportunity to become a significant producer - and ultimately exporter - of sustainable fuels, produced domestically using resources the country has in abundance rather than those it must import. A rising fuel bill can thus be turned into the foundation for a new export industry, helping to diversify revenue as Vision 2040 intends rather than trading one import dependency for another.

text:
K Shipbuilding and Lloyd’s Register (LR) on Monday (14 September) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to jointly develop an ethanol-fuelled 50,000 dwt Medium Range (MR) tanker.

Announced at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok, the joint development project will assess the technical feasibility, safety and regulatory compliance of a new ethanol-fuelled tanker design, with the objective of achieving Approval in Principle (AiP) from LR and creating a commercially competitive vessel concept for the global product tanker market.

LR will undertake technical reviews covering vessel arrangements, stability, structural requirements and fuel tank integration, while K Shipbuilding will lead the vessel design and development programme.

The project will also examine opportunities to optimise vessel design and operational efficiency while ensuring compliance with applicable class rules and international regulations.

Theo Kourmpelis, Global Business Director for tankers, Lloyd’s Register, said: “Ethanol is already a familiar cargo across the product tanker trades, which makes the MR segment a practical place to assess it as a fuel. As ethanol production and seaborne trade continue to develop, owners active in these trades are well placed to connect its role as a cargo with its use onboard.

“This project will give owners a clearer basis for evaluating ethanol within their fleet strategies, and help lay the groundwork for its broader uptake across the tanker sector.”

Andy McKeran, Chief Growth Officer, Lloyd’s Register, said: “Shipping’s energy transition is unlikely to be delivered through a single fuel solution. Shipowners are increasingly looking at a range of fuel options and want confidence that emerging technologies can be implemented safely, efficiently and in compliance with evolving regulations.

“This project will help deepen industry understanding of ethanol’s potential in the tanker sector and provide owners with greater insight into how alternative fuel solutions can be incorporated into commercially viable vessel designs.”

Tae-Hyun Koh, Chief Technology Officer, K Shipbuilding, said: “We see growing interest in fuel flexibility as shipowners make long-term investment decisions in an increasingly complex regulatory environment. Through this collaboration with Lloyd’s Register, we aim to develop a practical and competitive ethanol-fuelled MR tanker design that addresses both operational and market requirements.”

China’s Tangshan Maritime Safety Administration (MSA) on Thursday (10 September) conducted the country’s first dedicated emergency response exercise for a marine biofuel spill at Jingtang Port in Tangshan, Bohai Sea.

The “2026 Green Power Mission” exercise simulated a leak of 10 metric tonnes of biodiesel from a vessel experiencing a spill during cargo operations at a terminal.

Following the incident report, the Tangshan MSA’s vessel traffic management centre activated its emergency response procedures, issued a navigation warning and established a traffic control area.

The maritime patrol vessel Haixun 04501 arrived at the scene to coordinate the response, involving a drone unit, an oil spill response vessel and terminal emergency personnel.

A drone equipped with fluorescence detection equipment was deployed to identify the contaminated area. Terminal personnel used oil recovery equipment, while response vessels deployed containment booms to limit the spread of the spill and spraying equipment to remove the surface oil film.

The exercise also trialled the use of 355-nanometre ultraviolet light combined with drone-mounted fluorescence detection equipment to locate biodiesel contamination.

The Tangshan MSA said unlike conventional fuel oil, biodiesel spill traces can be difficult to identify by eye under natural light. The fluorescence detection system can identify biodiesel’s characteristic fluorescence signal, enabling responders to determine the spill boundary and support subsequent containment and recovery operations.

While biodiesel is biodegradable and has a lower sulphur content than conventional fuel oil, its behaviour following a spill and the methods required to detect it differ from those used for conventional oil spills, the MSA said.

The exercise tested response procedures covering incident reporting, aerial monitoring, surface containment, spill recovery and residual pollution removal.

The Tangshan MSA said it will use the exercise to improve biofuel spill emergency response plans, specialist training and equipment development as part of its “Green Bohai Sea” initiative.

The authority will also strengthen pollution risk prevention and accident response capabilities for vessels using new and clean energy fuels, it said.

Published: 16 September, 2026

Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore (BV) on Monday (14 September) said it awarded Approval in Principle (AiP) to Ningbo Kairong New Energy (Kairong) and Sweden-based MannTek for their jointly developed Ship-to-Ship LNG Bunkering Crane Master system at at Gastech 2026 in Bangkok.

Earlier the same day, Kairong and MannTek signed a Joint Development Cooperation Agreement and unveiled the latest Crane Master system.

Designed specifically for ship-to-ship LNG bunkering operations, the Crane Master is a multifunctional integrated bunkering and hoisting system that combines crane handling capabilities with LNG transfer functions in a single solution.

The design aims to address operational challenges associated with LNG bunkering in busy port environments by integrating bunkering and lifting operations while maintaining high standards of safety and operational efficiency.

As part of the approval process, BV conducted a review of the design in accordance with applicable classification requirements. The assessment focused on key aspects including LNG bunkering system safety principles, low temperature leakage protection, emergency shutdown and release arrangements, and spare-parts hoisting operations.

The AiP confirmed that the concept complies in principle with the relevant classification requirements and provides a foundation for further development and implementation.

“The certification highlights the growing importance of safe and reliable LNG bunkering infrastructure as the maritime industry advances its decarbonization journey,” BV said.

As LNG continues to play an important role as a transitional marine fuel, innovative bunkering solutions can help support the expansion of LNG fuel supply networks and the wider adoption of alternative fuels across the shipping industry.

title: EU loophole could dilute e-fuel target – industry and green groups - engine.online
description:
Getty Images The issue centres on the European Commission’s Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185 and how renewable hydrogen used as an intermediate input in biofuel production is accounted for.
The letter's immediate target is aviation's synthetic fuel supply obligation, but the signatories said the same accounting would carry over to shipping.
“This would allow existing biofuel refiners to claim they are delivering e-fuels, without building new synthetic fuel plants,” the letter said.
T&E said allowing this accounting approach could put that pipeline at risk and force the EU to import synthetic fuel to meet its own mandates.
The letter called for the same exclusion to be applied to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185.
text:
More than 20 organisations have urged EU lawmakers to close a “regulatory paradox” that could undermine future demand for synthetic marine fuels in a joint letter.

IMAGE: Illustration of vessel with an EU flag. Getty Images

The issue centres on the European Commission’s Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185 and how renewable hydrogen used as an intermediate input in biofuel production is accounted for.

The regulation does not clearly exclude electrolytic hydrogen used in the hydrotreatment of biofuels such as hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) from counting towards the synthetic fuel share of the resulting fuel, said the SASHA Coalition, a shipping and aviation industry alliance that signed the letter.

The letter's immediate target is aviation's synthetic fuel supply obligation, but the signatories said the same accounting would carry over to shipping.

This could blur the distinction between using green hydrogen as a processing input for biofuels and using it as a feedstock to produce synthetic fuels such as e-methanol and e-ammonia, which require dedicated production facilities.

“This would allow existing biofuel refiners to claim they are delivering e-fuels, without building new synthetic fuel plants,” the letter said.

FuelEU Maritime could mandate a 2% sub-target for synthetic e-fuels from 1 January 2034, if the EU Commission finds that these fuels account for less than 1% of the total energy used by ships covered by the regulation in 2031.

The sub-target would also not apply if the Commission finds that e-fuel production capacity, availability, geographical distribution or prices are inadequate, or if monitoring before 1 January 2033 shows the share is already above 2%.

The signatories argued that leaving the existing provision unchanged in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185 could allow biofuels produced using green hydrogen to count towards the future synthetic fuel sub-target requirement, potentially reducing demand for dedicated synthetic bunker fuel production.

This could weaken incentives for shipping companies and fuel suppliers to sign the long-term offtake agreements needed to finance new e-fuel projects and reach final investment decisions, the signatories warned.

Green group Transport & Environment (T&E), another signatory, counted 69 e-fuel projects in Europe that could supply the shipping sector, only six of them operational. T&E said allowing this accounting approach could put that pipeline at risk and force the EU to import synthetic fuel to meet its own mandates.

“…allowing this workaround introduces regulatory instability, signaling to market actors that EU rules can be diluted retroactively and opening a Pandora's box that permanently erodes trust in the long-term predictability of the EU regulatory framework,” the letter read.

The signatories want the Commission to address the issue by applying the same accounting approach it has already adopted for low-carbon fuels.

Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2359 excludes renewable fuels of non-biological origin used as intermediate products in the production of conventional fuels and biofuels when calculating the low-carbon share of the final fuel.

The letter called for the same exclusion to be applied to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185.

By Konica Bhatt and Gautamee Hazarika

title: SGMF: Methanol's GHG performance depends heavily on production pathway - safety4sea
description:
Production pathway is critical The assessment concludes that biogenic, renewable synthetic and industrial by-product synthetic methanol can deliver substantial GHG reductions compared with conventional fuels.
However, SGMF highlights significant variation in well-to-tank (WtT) emissions between production pathways.
Upstream production is the dominant factor determining lifecycle GHG intensity, while differences during marine engine use are comparatively smaller.
SGMF therefore says fossil-derived methanol should not be presented as a decarbonization option unless independently verified lifecycle GHG reductions are demonstrated.
For shipowners and other methanol users, SGMF recommends prioritizing traceable and certified, pathway-specific lifecycle GHG intensities when assessing fuel options.
text:
Conducted by WSP and critically peer reviewed by industry experts and academics, the “Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) study on the use of methanol as a marine fuel” study assesses 15 methanol production pathways in accordance with the IMO LCA Guidelines.

It considers emissions across the fuel life cycle and incorporates the performance of different marine engine types, including medium-speed four-stroke and low-speed two-stroke engines.

Production pathway is critical

The assessment concludes that biogenic, renewable synthetic and industrial by-product synthetic methanol can deliver substantial GHG reductions compared with conventional fuels. However, SGMF highlights significant variation in well-to-tank (WtT) emissions between production pathways.

Upstream production is the dominant factor determining lifecycle GHG intensity, while differences during marine engine use are comparatively smaller.

Key findings include:

Bio-methanol pathways have the lowest WtW GHG intensities among those assessed.

Synthetic methanol produced using renewable hydrogen can also achieve lower emissions.

Synthetic methanol using hydrogen generated as an industrial by-product can similarly deliver lower emissions.

Natural gas- and coal-derived methanol, including synthetic methanol produced using fossil hydrogen, remain materially positive on a WtW basis under the ISO baseline.

This remains the case even where carbon capture and storage (CCS) is applied.

SGMF therefore says fossil-derived methanol should not be presented as a decarbonization option unless independently verified lifecycle GHG reductions are demonstrated.

The organization also cautions that emerging pathways, particularly those involving direct air capture (DAC), electrolysis and some CCS-enabled configurations, carry greater uncertainty because of limited technology maturity and lifecycle inventory data.

Low-carbon inputs can change the picture

SGMF stresses that the study uses representative baseline pathways, rather than optimized or project-specific configurations.

As a result, actual supply chains using verified low-carbon inputs and dedicated renewable energy could achieve lower GHG intensities than those shown in the assessment.

For synthetic methanol in particular, the report identifies several factors as critical to lifecycle performance:

The origin and processing of hydrogen

The origin and processing of CO₂

The GHG intensity of electricity

The GHG intensity of steam

SGMF recommends prioritizing access to low-carbon electricity and, where possible, co-locating production facilities with low-carbon energy sources, hydrogen production and CO₂ supplies to reduce supply-chain emissions.

“SGMF is the only fuel-agnostic NGO with a proven track on providing clear and fact-based information to the maritime industry, covering technical and environmental aspects of future marine fuels. We therefore take pride in being the first organisation that conducted a high-quality full LCA on methanol as a marine fuel, complementing our portfolio of marine fuel LCAs,”

said Mark Bell, General Manager and COO of SGMF.

Implications for regulation and fuel supply

For regulators, SGMF recommends that regulatory frameworks incentivize methanol with the lowest GHG intensities by accounting for the factors that determine lifecycle performance. It also recommends:

Using conservative default emission factors that do not underestimate emissions.

Increasing the use of verified, pathway-specific data where available.

Expanding the IMO’s pathway framework to include commercially relevant production configurations that are not currently represented, including integrated production and co-processing arrangements, where transparent and verifiable pathway-specific lifecycle data are available.

The report also identifies lifecycle inventory data as a key constraint, particularly for synthetic methanol pathways, where results show the greatest variability and sensitivity.

Fuel suppliers and project developers are therefore encouraged to provide primary data from production facilities and supply chains and to document commercially deployed configurations.

For shipowners and other methanol users, SGMF recommends prioritizing traceable and certified, pathway-specific lifecycle GHG intensities when assessing fuel options.

The organization cautions, however, that the representative results should not be used without further consideration for individual investment or operational decisions, particularly where emerging production pathways involve significant uncertainty or data limitations.

Engine efficiency still matters

While the study found substantially greater variability in WtT emissions than in tank-to-wake (TtW) emissions, SGMF says engine manufacturers still have a role to play in reducing the overall lifecycle footprint.

The report recommends:

Continued improvements in engine efficiency

Reducing the pilot-fuel energy fraction required across the engine duty cycle, including at 10% load

Reducing urea consumption

SGMF also stresses that the findings should not be interpreted as a ranking of optimized methanol production routes.

The assessment deliberately applies the IMO-prescribed pathway configurations and cautious assumptions to support policy and regulatory discussions, including the potential development of default emission factors.

Consequently, differences between pathways that fall within the study’s significance thresholds, or where uncertainty remains high, should not be overstated. SGMF says comparative conclusions should be drawn only where differences are sufficiently large and methodologically robust.

Completing SGMF’s alternative-fuel LCA portfolio

The methanol assessment completes SGMF’s current portfolio of LCAs covering LNG, ammonia and methanol.

It follows:

SGMF’s third-edition LNG LCA, released earlier in 2026

SGMF’s inaugural ammonia LCA, published in 2024

The new methanol LCA, published in 2026

SGMF said the three studies provide stakeholders with a science-based basis for examining the emissions performance of key alternative marine fuels.

However, it stressed that LCAs represent a snapshot of industry performance at a particular point in time and will need to be updated as fuel-production technologies, supply chains and GHG-intensity data evolve.

text:
The Port of Barcelona is among the eleven promoting ports of the Busan Port Declaration 2026, an international declaration signed by some of the main port infrastructures in the world, aimed at advancing innovation, enhancing the resilience of global logistics chains, and accelerating the energy transition of maritime transport and port infrastructures. The text was adopted at the meeting of port executives held in Busan (South Korea), coinciding with the 150th anniversary of the commissioning of the Korean port.

The declaration sets commitments on data interoperability and digital collaboration between ports, the application of artificial intelligence to logistics chain management, the promotion of sustainable fuels and low-emission technologies, and the exchange of knowledge and best practices among ports worldwide. In this regard, the document explicitly mentions the International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) as key platforms for articulating that cooperation.

Barcelona was one of the few European ports invited to the CEOs meeting, where it shared a table with representatives such as Rotterdam, Los Angeles, and Hamburg. Its president, José Alberto Carbonell, participated on Monday in that meeting along with representatives from the ports of Busan, Rotterdam, Los Angeles, Hamburg, Antwerp-Bruges, HAROPA, Singapore, Long Beach, Seattle, and Ningbo. During the session, the port leaders presented their vision on the main challenges facing the maritime and logistics sector in a scenario conditioned by climate change, geopolitical uncertainty, rising protectionism, and technological advancements, including AI, which reshape global supply chains and transform the role of ports.

"The Busan Declaration highlights that the major challenges of the maritime sector can only be addressed through international cooperation," said Carbonell, who called on ports to work together in digitalization, resilience of logistics chains, and accelerating decarbonization.

On Tuesday, the president of the Port of Barcelona spoke at the fourteenth edition of the Busan International Port Conference (BIPC), one of the main international meetings of the Asian port sector. Carbonell, accompanied by the director of Institutional Relations of the port, Ingrid Boqué, participated in the session dedicated to decarbonization, where he presented the Catalan experience in the deployment of the wharf electrification system (Onshore Power Supply, OPS), one of the central actions of his energy transition strategy.

In his speech, he explained the methodology that the Port of Barcelona uses to quantify greenhouse gas emissions and noted that moored ships represent a significant part of port emissions, which makes the electrification of wharves one of the measures with the highest potential for reducing environmental impact.

Carbonell detailed the investments that the infrastructure develops through Nexigen, its wharf electrification plan, to make that energy transformation possible. He also outlined the technical and economic challenges linked to the simultaneous connection of large ships at the same wharf, an operation that requires a high capacity of electrical supply.

The president argued that wharf electrification represents a strategic and competitive long-term solution towards more sustainable ports, complementary to the deployment of new decarbonized fuels, and positioned the economic viability of investments as a condition for accelerating sector decarbonization. "The OPS deployment and the commitment to electrification are a fundamental step towards building the emission-neutral port that society demands from us," he asserted.

The Busan International Port Conference brings together port authorities and operators from Asia, Europe, and North America each year, and the declaration adopted in 2026 groups ports from those three continents around the working frameworks of the IAPH and the IMO.

title: Hamburg Port Authority: Shore power will play an increasing role in maritime electrification
description:
Shore power remains a central part of this strategy.
Learning from early implementation Hamburg’s own experience with shore power has changed significantly over time.
“Very often many people have regarded shore power as a transitional activity, and we definitely think shore power is here to stay,” he said.
For Hamburg Port Authority, this means that shore power will increasingly form part of a broader electrification strategy rather than simply serving as an emissions-reduction measure while ships are alongside.
Shore power will play an increasing role in the electrification and decarbonization of the industry, in our view he concluded.
text:
Speaking with SAFETY4SEA during SMM 2026, held from September 1 to 4 in Hamburg, Hanno Bromeis, Head of Port Energy Solutions at Hamburg Port Authority, highlighted the importance of combining infrastructure development with close collaboration across ports, terminals and shipping companies.

Building energy infrastructure towards 2030

Bromeis explained that Hamburg Port Authority’s energy strategy is guided by Fit for 55 requirements, while also taking into account the economic realities of major infrastructure investments.

We are guided by the Fit for 55 regulation, so that is basically what leads us, and we want to be compliant and therefore do everything that it takes,

he said.

Shore power remains a central part of this strategy. Hamburg has already developed facilities for cruise ships and large container vessels, while short-sea shipping is the next area of focus.

“We actually continue to build our OPS facilities. We’ve done so for the cruise market and the large container vessels, and now basically short sea is next,” Bromeis explained.

However, shore power is only one part of the wider energy transition taking place within the port.

In parallel, Hamburg is seeking to increase renewable energy generation within the port itself, supported where appropriate by energy storage facilities and stronger grid infrastructure.

“All this in tandem is actually the challenge that lies ahead of us and that we’re trying to fulfil till 2030,” he said.

Hamburg as a testing ground

Bromeis described Hamburg as an early mover in shore power and said the port’s experience can provide useful lessons for others developing similar infrastructure.

“We pride ourselves on being a frontrunner in shore power, so we very much see ourselves as a leading port and a big testing ground for the industry,” he said.

Hamburg has therefore encouraged representatives from other ports and terminals to visit and learn from the experience gained during implementation.

For Bromeis, this exchange of knowledge is particularly important because the scale of maritime decarbonization means that individual ports cannot address the transition in isolation.

“It’s a massive challenge for the overall industry, and that only works if we collaborate,” he said. “Therefore, exchange is key.”

Industry events such as SMM also play a role in this process by providing opportunities to share operational experience, challenges and lessons learned.

Learning from early implementation

Hamburg’s own experience with shore power has changed significantly over time.

Bromeis recalled that when the port first started developing its infrastructure, there was far less industry experience available and many solutions had to be tested in practice.

“When we started, there wasn’t any industry yet, so we had to figure things out ourselves a lot,” he said.

Today, however, more ports have implemented shore power facilities, creating a larger pool of practical knowledge that can help others avoid repeating the same learning process.

I would always recommend looking and talking to other people that have done it already, because there are now ports that have implemented facilities already and you can learn from them a lot

…Bromeis said.

The next step, he added, is to involve customers, shipping companies and other ports early in the process.

“Cooperation is probably the single most important factor that you need to be doing once you have the funding in place and can officially get started.”

Shore power is here to stay

One misconception Bromeis would like to challenge is the idea that shore power is only a temporary solution during shipping’s transition towards lower-emission fuels and technologies.

“Very often many people have regarded shore power as a transitional activity, and we definitely think shore power is here to stay,” he said.

While shore power initially emerged primarily as a way of reducing emissions from vessels at berth, Bromeis expects its role to expand as ships themselves become increasingly electrified.

“We will see a different period where we are expecting fully electric vessels or more electrified vessels,” he explained.

He pointed in particular to the feeder segment, where Hamburg expects the first fully electric container vessels to begin arriving around 2028.

“We expect the first fully electric container vessels coming in ’28, and we actually will charge them on a shore power facility,” Bromeis said.

For Hamburg Port Authority, this means that shore power will increasingly form part of a broader electrification strategy rather than simply serving as an emissions-reduction measure while ships are alongside.

As ports prepare for this next phase, Bromeis highlighted infrastructure development, grid capacity and industry cooperation as key factors in supporting the transition.

Shore power will play an increasing role in the electrification and decarbonization of the industry, in our view

he concluded.

text:
Yokogawa Electric Corporation has secured orders from Kawasaki Heavy Industries to supply integrated automation systems for the world’s largest liquefied hydrogen carrier, with a capacity of 40,000 m³, as well as two hydrogen-fuelled vessels. The projects will support safer hydrogen transport and help advance the development of a large-scale liquefied hydrogen supply chain.

Supporting safe hydrogen transport

As hydrogen adoption grows, safe and efficient storage and transportation of large volumes are becoming increasingly important. Liquefied hydrogen, transported at extremely low temperatures, is expected to play a key role in building this supply chain.

For the 40,000 m³ carrier, Yokogawa will provide an integrated system to monitor and control onboard equipment, along with emergency shutdown functions. The technology is designed to support safe and reliable vessel operations while improving equipment performance and reducing crew workload throughout the vessel’s lifecycle.

Also Read: Hirata brings semiconductor equipment portfolio to India

Enabling hydrogen-fuelled shipping

Yokogawa will also supply integrated automation systems for marine hydrogen fuel systems (MHFS) on two hydrogen-fuelled vessels. These systems include liquefied hydrogen tanks and fuel supply equipment, which are key technologies for reducing emissions from maritime transport.

The vessels are being developed under a Green Innovation Fund project led by Japan’s New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO). The project aims to support safe, large-scale maritime hydrogen transportation and contribute to the wider development of the liquefied hydrogen supply chain.

Koji Nakaoka, Yokogawa Electric executive vice president & executive officer and head of the company’s Energy & Sustainability Business Headquarters, commented, “Yokogawa has extensive experience with liquefied natural gas carriers, and our technology is also being applied to liquefied hydrogen carriers. Leveraging the technologies and expertise we have developed in the field of control and safety instrumentation, we will continue to provide solutions that support safe and reliable operations for our customers in the energy sector, including hydrogen.”

text:
In Cyprus, Cyprus Mail reported that International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez described 2026 as a difficult year for global shipping. According to him, the industry has faced challenges due to geopolitical conflicts and disruptions to global supply chains.

Losses among seafarers

In an address for World Maritime Day, Dominguez said that too many seafarers had died as a result of geopolitical conflicts. He noted that the organization’s thoughts are first and foremost with the affected seafarers and their families.

The IMO Secretary-General also said that global energy and food supply chains had been disrupted. According to him, the organization will provide shipping and seafarers with firm and consistent support.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

From policy to practice

The theme of World Maritime Day 2026 is “From policy to practice, powering maritime excellence.” Dominguez explained that rules can make shipping safer, more sustainable and cleaner only if they are implemented worldwide. The IMO seeks to support member states in effectively implementing its regulations so that they can benefit from the opportunities of the next decade. Among such opportunities, Dominguez named digitalization, responding to the energy transition, and expanding opportunities for women to create a more inclusive and diverse maritime sector.

For World Maritime Day, IMO headquarters is to be illuminated in blue as a symbol of the transition from policy to practice. The organization also called on member states and international and non-governmental organizations to join the initiative.

title: Getting to Zero Coalition calls on IMO Member States to secure an investable Net-Zero Framework
description:
As negotiators work to finalise a text, the Getting to Zero Coalition believes the priority must be for the IMO to urgently adopt a framework that can support a globally inclusive and investable transition.
Targeted support for lower-income countries will therefore remain an important part of a framework that is effective, just, and equitable.
The framework must also instil confidence in those companies seeking to make early investments in long-term, zero-emission fuels and technologies.
Only this can create an investable environment that allows long-term fuels to grow and develop alongside readily available but potentially less scalable fuels.
Ahead of the next round of discussions later this year, the Getting to Zero Coalition urges IMO Member States to keep these outcomes at the centre of the negotiations.
text:
The Getting to Zero Coalition welcomes continued efforts to find common ground on a global framework for shipping’s energy transition, following the 22nd session of the International Maritime Organization’s Intersessional Working Group on the Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships .

Discussions last week revisited the postponed IMO Net-Zero Framework and considered a broader range of proposals and possible approaches, including the design and ambition of the greenhouse gas fuel-intensity trajectory, compliance mechanisms, reward structures, and fund governance. As negotiators work to finalise a text, the Getting to Zero Coalition believes the priority must be for the IMO to urgently adopt a framework that can support a globally inclusive and investable transition.

To be globally inclusive and investable, the transition must minimise the risk of regional fragmentation, create accessible and efficient investment opportunities for companies and countries with diverse circumstances, and address the concerns of countries that may be disproportionately affected. Targeted support for lower-income countries will therefore remain an important part of a framework that is effective, just, and equitable.

The framework must also instil confidence in those companies seeking to make early investments in long-term, zero-emission fuels and technologies. In the coming years, thousands of new vessels will be ordered, locking in investment decisions that will shape the transition well beyond the next decade. First movers need strong incentives to act. Their investments will set the table for a market-wide transition.

This means ambitious and fixed targets for the near and long term, a stable credit market, and predictable reward mechanisms that can help reduce the risk of committing to zero-emission fuels and technologies before they reach scale. Only this can create an investable environment that allows long-term fuels to grow and develop alongside readily available but potentially less scalable fuels.

During the next phase of work, the objective should remain clear: a high-ambition, predictable framework that enables the industry to invest early, drives a cost-effective transition, supports first movers, and creates the conditions for long-term, zero-emission fuels and technologies to reach scale in time.

Ahead of the next round of discussions later this year, the Getting to Zero Coalition urges IMO Member States to keep these outcomes at the centre of the negotiations.

title: Weak Sustainable Fuel Rules Risk Carbon Burden: EDF - Mexico Business News
description:
Global expansion of sustainable alternative fuels risks creating hidden carbon liabilities and secondary environmental damage without strict, internationally harmonized lifecycle emissions standards across their entire value chain.
EDF emphasizes that clean fuel diversification encompassing domestic hydrogen, e-fuels, and sustainable biofuels presents an opportunity for nations to reduce reliance on volatile fossil fuel import markets while stabilizing industrial inputs and expanding export capacity.
According to EDF, the appeal of clean fuel diversification, encompassing domestic hydrogen, e-fuels, and sustainable biofuels, stems from its capacity to reduce national reliance on volatile fossil fuel import markets while stabilizing industrial inputs.
These low-emissions fuels target hard-to-abate sectors, including heavy trucking, maritime shipping, aviation, steel, cement, and chemical manufacturing, which together account for roughly one-third of global carbon emissions.

text:
Global expansion of sustainable alternative fuels risks creating hidden carbon liabilities and secondary environmental damage without strict, internationally harmonized lifecycle emissions standards across their entire value chain. Establishing science-based compliance frameworks through international bodies like ICAO and the IMO is critical for hard-to-abate sectors, including aviation, shipping, heavy transport, and manufacturing, to ensure alternative fuel investments deliver genuine decarbonization. Transparent accounting from feedstock sourcing to end-use combustion protects market integrity, prevents regulatory fragmentation, and ensures capital flows into genuinely low-impact energy pathways.

____

The Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) published a peer-reviewed position calling for the adoption of internationally harmonized sustainability standards to govern the global expansion of alternative energy sources.

EDF emphasizes that clean fuel diversification encompassing domestic hydrogen, e-fuels, and sustainable biofuels presents an opportunity for nations to reduce reliance on volatile fossil fuel import markets while stabilizing industrial inputs and expanding export capacity. However, research published by the group in Environmental Science & Technology highlights that sustainability is not an inherent property of any fuel molecule, but rather a function of its entire value chain, including feedstock sourcing, energy inputs, production efficiency, transport, and combustion.

According to EDF, the appeal of clean fuel diversification, encompassing domestic hydrogen, e-fuels, and sustainable biofuels, stems from its capacity to reduce national reliance on volatile fossil fuel import markets while stabilizing industrial inputs. These low-emissions fuels target hard-to-abate sectors, including heavy trucking, maritime shipping, aviation, steel, cement, and chemical manufacturing, which together account for roughly one-third of global carbon emissions.

However, EDF considers that uncoordinated execution presents distinct environmental risks across different production pathways. Biofuels derived from crops grown on recently converted forest land can emit more carbon dioxide than the petroleum fuels they replace, alongside negative impacts on biodiversity and water resources. Natural gas-derived hydrogen produced without high carbon capture rates, permanent geologic storage, or strict upstream methane controls offers little climate benefit, while e-fuels manufactured with fossil-intensive electricity carry hidden carbon and air-quality burdens.

To prevent regulatory fragmentation and protect global market stability, EDF proposes a policy framework focused on direct electrification powered by new renewable energy sources as the primary decarbonization mechanism, reserving alternative fuels strictly for applications where direct electrification is not technically feasible. The framework mandates transparent lifecycle emissions accounting for every fuel pathway, targeted incentives for low-impact production, and operational controls to eliminate fugitive emissions of methane, hydrogen, and ammonia.

Through observer status at international regulatory forums, including the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO), EDF engages directly with industry and government stakeholders to establish unified, science-led compliance standards. “We are using our science-led approach to proactively find the solutions that work for the entire ecosystem, and we’re ready to engage with all stakeholders to get this right,” reads EDF’s website.

Opportunities for Mexico's Clean Energy Leadership

In an MBN Expert Contributor piece, Leonardo Beltrán, Non-Resident Fellow, Institute of the Americas, notes that clean power functions as a strategic lever for regional energy security, industrial competitiveness, and geopolitical resilience. Beltrán considers that Mexico has competitive wind and solar resources, integrated supply chains, and preferential North American market access, positioning the country to transition from a clean technology adopter to a regional energy hub. Addressing exchange rate volatility and financial risks is essential to support this transition, as major public energy entities like PEMEX and CFE faced substantial foreign exchange losses in early 2025. He considers that deploying innovative financial mechanisms, such as the proposed Clean Energy Exchange Rate Coverage Facility (ERCF) developed by researchers at Columbia University, the World Bank, and the World Economic Forum, could protect clean energy investments from currency depreciation without distorting market incentives.

Furthermore, Beltrán emphasizes three core levers to maximize regional clean energy integration: regulatory harmonization, certification systems, and cross-border grid interconnections. Aligning technical standards can replicate historical industrial gains, such as the growth in refrigerator manufacturing under NAFTA. Participation in CertHiLAC, a regional green hydrogen certification system supported by GIZ, OLADE, and the IDB, provides the transparent emissions tracking required to access European and Asian markets. “Mexico has the natural resources, industrial base, and market access to lead. What is needed now is an intentional strategy: aligning our diplomacy, finance, and domestic policy to drive investment, create jobs, and enhance energy security,” Beltrán concludes.
