text:
Abstract

Livestock carriers contribute to greenhouse gas emissions through the continued use of conventional fossil fuels. This study presents a theoretical, steady-state case study of replacing the Wärtsilä W7X35 diesel engine of the livestock carrier Motor Vessel MV Ganado Express with a Wärtsilä 46F methanol-fueled engine (7500 kW, operated at 81.2% load to deliver the required 6090 kW), using published specific fuel consumption values and emission factors. Fuel consumption and exhaust emissions were estimated with a bottom-up method over a 24 h sailing period, and the annual well-to-wake (WtW) greenhouse gas fuel intensity (GFI) and compliance costs were assessed for 2028–2035 against the two-tier targets of the IMO Net-Zero Framework approved at MEPC 83. Because methanol is a carbon-bearing fuel, tank-to-wake carbon dioxide emissions are nearly unchanged, declining by only 5.4%, whereas nitrogen oxide emissions fall by 73.2% and sulfur oxide emissions are eliminated. The decarbonization benefit arises instead on a well-to-wake basis: with renewable e-methanol, annual lifecycle emissions fall from 29,897 to 2291 tCO2eq. Diesel operation exceeds both targets from 2028, at a compliance cost rising from USD 0.91 to 3.85 million per year, while e-methanol remains in direct compliance throughout the period. E-methanol nevertheless remains the more expensive option, the annual cost gap narrowing from USD 15.1 to 12.2 million by 2035.

1. Introduction

Climate change has become one of the most critical global challenges of the twenty-first century. Increasing atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases from fossil fuel combustion have accelerated global warming and contributed to severe environmental consequences, including rising sea levels, extreme weather events, and deteriorating air quality [1]. Maritime transportation plays a crucial role in international trade, carrying over 80% of the volume of world merchandise trade and serving as the backbone of the world economy [2,3]. However, the shipping sector remains a significant contributor to atmospheric emissions [4].

Total shipping emitted 1056 million tonnes of CO2 in 2018, about 2.89% of global anthropogenic CO2 emissions [5], along with substantial amounts of nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur oxides (SOx), and particulate matter. These pollutants negatively impact both environmental sustainability and human health [6,7]. Previous studies show that maritime transport accounts for about 15% of global NOx emissions and 11% of global SOx emissions, highlighting the urgent need for cleaner propulsion technologies [8].

To address these environmental concerns, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has introduced increasingly stringent regulations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from ships [9,10]. According to the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Ships, IMO aims to reduce the carbon intensity of international shipping by at least 40% by 2030 relative to 2008 levels. In addition, total annual greenhouse gas emissions are targeted to decrease by at least 20% by 2030 and by at least 70% by 2040, with targets of 30% and 80%, respectively.

The long-term objective is to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. Achieving these ambitious goals requires adopting alternative fuels and innovative propulsion technologies to reduce the environmental footprint of maritime operations [11,12]. Recently, attention has increased on assessing Greenhouse Gas Fuel Intensity (GFI) as a key indicator of the environmental performance of marine fuels. Unlike conventional emission metrics that consider only onboard combustion emissions, GFI adopts a life-cycle perspective by accounting for both Well-to-Tank and Tank-to-Wake greenhouse gas emissions.

This approach provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the carbon intensity associated with different fuels and supports the transition toward low- and zero-carbon energy sources. In line with the International Maritime Organization’s strategy to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, GFI assessment has become an essential component of comparing alternative fuels and determining their potential contribution to maritime decarbonization. Beyond its environmental significance, Greenhouse GFI has important economic implications under the International Maritime Organization’s Net-Zero Framework.

To support the transition toward net-zero emissions, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 a two-tier Greenhouse GFI compliance framework, the IMO Net-Zero Framework, as a new chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI, circulated for adoption as part of a draft revised consolidated Annex VI [13]. The second extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee adjourned its adoption in October 2025 [14], and the resumed session is scheduled for December 2026 [15].

This analysis therefore uses the target values and pricing in the approved draft text; the 2028 start of the first reporting period and the 2031–2035 trajectory depend on the outcome of that session. The framework is based on a 2008 reference value of 93.3 gCO2eq/MJ. Beginning in 2028, ships will be assessed against two annual reduction targets: a Base Target and a more stringent Direct Compliance Target (Regulation 35). For 2028, these targets correspond to reductions of 4% and 17%, resulting in GFI limits of 89.57 and 77.44 gCO2eq/MJ, respectively, rising to 30% and 43% by 2035 (65.31 and 53.18 gCO2eq/MJ). Ships achieving a GFI value equal to or below the Direct Compliance Target are considered in direct compliance and receive Surplus Units (SUs), which can be banked or transferred.

Vessels with attained GFI values between the Direct Compliance Target and the Base Target accrue a Tier 1 GFI compliance deficit, which is balanced through remedial units priced at USD 100 per tonne of CO2eq. Ships exceeding the Base Target accrue both a Tier 1 deficit, for the emissions between the Base and Direct Compliance targets, and a Tier 2 deficit, for the emissions above the Base Target, balanced through surplus units or remedial units priced at USD 380 per tonne of CO2eq (Regulations 36.4 to 36.9); these prices apply to the reporting periods 2028 to 2030, and the pricing mechanism for 2031 onwards is to be determined by the Committee by 1 January 2028 (Regulation 36.10). Consequently, reducing the GFI of marine fuels now affects environmental objectives, future compliance costs, and the economic competitiveness of shipping operations alike [16].

To reduce NOx emissions from ships, IMO introduced MARPOL Annex VI, Regulation 13, which is specifically designed to control NOx release from marine diesel engines. This regulation is applicable to engines with a power output greater than 130 kW and is mandatory for vessels constructed on or after 1 January 2000. NOx emission control is structured into three progressive standards: Tier I, Tier II, and Tier III, applicable to ships constructed from 2000, 2011, and 2016, respectively; the last only within NOx emission control areas. These tiers define emission limits as a function of engine rotational speed (n), as illustrated in Figure 1.

Figure 1. NOx emission limits of Regulation 13 of MARPOL Annex VI as a function of rated engine speed, with the Tier II and Tier III values at the rated speeds of the two engines compared in this study.

For a ship constructed in 2013, Tier II applies. The replacement of an engine by a non-identical marine diesel engine is, however, a major conversion to which the standards in force at the time of replacement apply (Regulation 13.2.2): a replacement engine installed today must meet Tier III when operating in a NOx Tier III emission control area, and only where it is not possible for such an engine to meet Tier III does Tier II apply, taking into account the guidelines developed by the Organization [17], the Administration having to notify the Organization whenever a Tier II rather than a Tier III replacement engine has been installed on or after 1 August 2025 [13].

Among the available alternatives, e-methanol has emerged as one of the most promising marine fuels [18]. Unlike conventional marine diesel oil, methanol contains virtually no sulfur, resulting in negligible SOx emissions during combustion. Additionally, methanol combustion can significantly reduce NOx emissions while offering simpler storage and handling requirements compared with hydrogen-based systems. Methanol can be stored as a liquid under ambient conditions, eliminating the need for cryogenic storage systems and reducing retrofitting complexity.

Livestock vessels are an important segment of the maritime transportation sector, supporting the global supply chain of animal products that meet the increasing demand for meat and protein. As the world’s population continues to grow and living standards improve, the demand for livestock-derived foods is expected to rise considerably. Komarek et al. [19] projected that global demand for livestock-derived foods in 2050 would be approximately 38% higher than in 2020, primarily due to population growth and rising incomes.

Consequently, the role of livestock carriers in ensuring food security and supplying animal products is expected to become increasingly important. Given the anticipated expansion of this sector, improving the environmental performance of livestock vessels and reducing greenhouse gas emissions are essential for achieving sustainable maritime transportation [20].

Methanol propulsion systems offer a more straightforward transition pathway because they can be integrated into existing marine engine platforms with relatively minor modifications [21]. Furthermore, methanol is already available as a commodity at more than 100 ports worldwide, although far fewer ports have established bunkering procedures [22].

The present study evaluates the environmental and regulatory performance of replacing the conventional Wärtsilä W7X35 diesel engine installed onboard MV Ganado Express with a Wärtsilä 46F methanol engine. The analysis focuses on fuel consumption, carbon dioxide, NOx, and SOx emissions over a 24 h sailing period while maintaining the vessel’s original propulsion power requirement, as well as well-to-wake greenhouse gas fuel intensity and compliance costs under the IMO Net-Zero Framework.

Previous diesel–methanol engine comparisons have addressed container ships, ferries and fishing vessels [21,23] and, for livestock carriers, methane emissions from the cargo and hydrogen fuel cells [20,24]. To the authors’ knowledge, no study has assessed methanol propulsion for a livestock carrier, nor quantified the Tier 1 and Tier 2 compliance deficits of the IMO Net-Zero Framework for this ship type.

The contribution of this work is threefold: (i) a consistent, fully documented steady-state comparison of diesel and methanol operation for a real livestock carrier at the same delivered power; (ii) an explicit separation between tank-to-wake exhaust emissions and well-to-wake GHG intensity, which locates the decarbonization benefit of methanol in the latter; and (iii) a year-by-year compliance-cost assessment for 2028–2035 following the definitions of the draft revised MARPOL Annex VI, including a sensitivity analysis on the e-methanol GHG intensity.

2. Materials and Methods

The livestock carrier MV Ganado Express was selected as the case study vessel, following a previous study by the group on alternative fuels for an existing vessel [25]. Cosco Guangdong Shipyard in China built the vessel in 2013, and it is currently used for international livestock transport. The ship is designed to transport cattle, sheep, horses, goats, and other livestock while complying with international animal welfare standards. The vessel has five livestock decks totaling approximately 4511 m2 of livestock area and can accommodate approximately 4000 cattle. With a gross tonnage of 10,421, the vessel falls within the scope of chapter 5 of the draft revised MARPOL Annex VI, which applies to ships of 5000 GT and above (Regulation 30) [13].

The original propulsion system consists of a Wärtsilä W7X35 diesel engine (Wärtsilä Corporation, Helsinki, Finland) with a maximum continuous rating of 6090 kW. In this study, we replace the original engine with a Wärtsilä 46F methanol-fueled engine (Wärtsilä Corporation, Helsinki, Finland) in theory, while maintaining the same propulsion power requirement. Table 1 shows the Characteristics of MV Ganado Express.

Table 1. Characteristics of MV Ganado Express.

The original propulsion engine onboard MV Ganado Express is a Wärtsilä W7X35 low-speed (Wärtsilä Corporation, Helsinki, Finland), two-stroke marine diesel engine, directly coupled to the propeller at 167 rpm. Table 2 presents the engine specifications [26].

Table 2. Diesel engine specifications [26].

This study considers the Wärtsilä 46F Methanol Engine (Wärtsilä Corporation, Helsinki, Finland), a four-stroke, non-reversible, medium-speed engine delivering 1250 kW per cylinder at 600 rpm in methanol mode [27]. The selected six-cylinder in-line engine has a rated output of 7500 kW. Because the vessel requires only 6090 kW, the engine is assumed to operate at 81.2% of its rated capacity. The Wärtsilä 46F was selected because it is a commercially available methanol-capable engine in the required power range and belongs to a platform with a long operational record, offering a practical decarbonization pathway without requiring major modifications to ship operational practices [27,28]. Table 3 shows the specifications of the Wärtsilä 46F Methanol Engine [27,29].

Table 3. Specifications of the Wärtsilä 6L46F Methanol engine [27,29].

The two engines differ in kind. The W7X35 is a two-stroke, low-speed, reversible engine coupled directly to a fixed-pitch propeller at 167 rpm, whereas the 46F is a four-stroke, non-reversible, medium-speed engine rated at 600 rpm. Delivering 6090 kW to the same propeller therefore requires a reduction gearbox with a ratio of approximately 3.6:1 and, because the 46F is non-reversible, either a controllable-pitch propeller or a reversing gear. The engine-room arrangement would need to accommodate the gearbox and thrust bearing, a new foundation and shaft line, the methanol fuel supply system with double-walled piping, ventilation and inerting of tank and fuel-preparation spaces, and fire detection and extinguishing arrangements suitable for a low-flashpoint fuel, in accordance with the IMO interim guidelines for ships using methyl/ethyl alcohol as fuel [30]. Because methanol has roughly half the lower calorific value of diesel (19.9 versus 42.7 MJ/kg) and a lower density (792 versus up to 890 kg/m3 at 15 °C for grade DMA under ISO 8217), its volumetric energy density is 15.8 against 38.0 MJ/L, so the same endurance requires about 2.4 times the tank volume, and the cofferdam separation required for methanol tanks further reduces the usable volume.

The 6L46F has a dry mass of 97 t and overall dimensions of 8620 × 2905 × 3500 mm (length × width × height, rigidly mounted, without flywheel) [29], which must be compared with the space released by removing the W7X35 and with the additional volume required by the gearbox, the methanol fuel supply system and the tank arrangement. A detailed retrofit assessment covering stability, structural integration, tank arrangement, class approval and cost is outside the scope of this study, which is confined to the environmental and regulatory comparison of the two engines at the same operating point.

The methanol specific fuel consumption of 375 g/kWh corresponds to 174.8 g/kWh of diesel-equivalent fuel (375 × 19.9/42.7). This is within 1.2% of the guaranteed consumption of the diesel version of the same engine at the closest tabulated operating point, 176.8 g/kWh on light fuel oil at 85% load for the main-engine controllable-pitch variable-speed configuration under ISO conditions [29], which supports the assumed value on an energy-equivalent basis. The Product Guide reports consumption of 176.8, 181.1, and 183.1 g/kWh at 85%, 75%, and 50% load, respectively, so specific consumption varies by less than 4% over that range, and a constant value is a reasonable assumption for a steady-state comparison at a single operating point.

No manufacturer consumption curve has been published for methanol mode: the manufacturer states that engine conversion technology for the 46F is not yet available and is still in development [22], so no in-service consumption data exist for this engine on methanol. The value used here is therefore an assumption of the study, and the sensitivity of the results to it is limited to the fuel-cost term, since the emission results depend on the fuel consumed rather than on the engine that consumes it.

Emission factors quantify pollutant emissions produced during engine operation. Table 4 presents the fuel properties, tank-to-wake emission factors, and well-to-wake GHG intensity for both engine types: the conventional diesel engine and the methanol engine. The lower calorific value (LCV) and the carbon conversion factors (Cf) of marine gas oil are taken from Appendix 2 of the 2024 IMO LCA Guidelines [31] and those of methanol from Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 [32]; the tank-to-wake CO2 emission factor of each fuel is derived from its specific fuel consumption and its Cf, which makes Table 4 and Table 5 consistent by construction.

Table 4. Fuel properties, tank-to-wake emission factors and well-to-wake GHG intensity.

Table 5. Fuel consumption and tank-to-wake emissions of diesel and methanol engines.

The NOx factors are study assumptions rather than certified values: engine manufacturers publish compliance with a NOx tier rather than a certified emission value, and the methanol version of the 46F is not yet in service, so no measured figure is available for either engine. The 11.2 g/kWh assumed for the W7X35 lies below the Tier II limit of 13.56 g/kWh applicable at its rated speed, as is required of an engine certified in 2013, and the 3.0 g/kWh assumed for the 46F is consistent with the manufacturer’s statement that Tier III compliance of that engine is achieved with a selective catalytic reduction system [27], which places its engine-out emission above the Tier III limit of 2.50 g/kWh and well below the Tier II limit of 10.10 g/kWh at 600 rpm.

The SOx factor is derived from the sulfur balance of the fuel: complete oxidation of the fuel sulfur gives 2 g of SO2 per gram of sulfur burned, so that for marine gas oil meeting the 0.10% m/m limit applicable in sulfur oxide emission control areas under Regulation 14 of MARPOL Annex VI [13], the emission factor is 2 × 0.001 × 170 = 0.34 g/kWh. Methanol contains no sulfur, so no SOx emission factor is required for it.

The well-to-wake GFI values of Table 4 are lifecycle indicators; they are not exhaust emissions and are used only for the Net-Zero Framework assessment. For marine gas oil the WtW intensity is built on the IMO basis: the well-to-tank default of 17.7 gCO2eq/MJ given in Appendix 2 of the LCA Guidelines, plus the tank-to-wake term computed with the Guidelines’ own formula from the Cf factors of the same table, the LCV of 0.0427 MJ/g and the AR5 GWP100 values (28 for CH4 and 265 for N2O), which gives 76.2 gCO2eq/MJ and a total of 93.9 gCO2eq/MJ [31]. For comparison, the FuelEU Maritime default for the same fuel is 90.77 gCO2eq/MJ (WtT 14.4 plus TtW 76.37 with AR4 GWP values) [32]; the difference arises from the upstream term and from the GWP set.

The e-methanol value of 7 gCO2eq/MJ corresponds to methanol synthesized from hydrogen produced by electrolysis with renewable electricity and CO2 obtained by direct air capture or industrial carbon capture, on a well-to-wake boundary in which the combustion CO2 is counted in the tank-to-wake term and offset by the emission credit for the captured CO2 used as carbon stock (term e_ccu with SF_ccu = 1, the “TtW value 2” of paragraph 5.3 of the Guidelines) [31]. This pathway is listed in Appendix 1 of the Guidelines as MeOH_rCO2_rH2_MS_gm (no. 96) but has no default emission factor in Appendix 2, so we bound the value from external sources. Du et al. [33] optimized this production route at seven EU ports and report lifecycle GHG emission savings of 95.96% for the configurations supplied entirely by offshore wind, which corresponds to 3.8 gCO2eq/MJ against the fossil comparator of 94 gCO2eq/MJ; the European methodology for renewable fuels of non-biological origin requires a minimum saving of 70%, equivalent to 28.2 gCO2eq/MJ [34]. These two values are computed under the European methodology, whose system boundary, comparator, and global warming potentials differ from those of the IMO LCA Guidelines, so they are not IMO GFI values and are used here only as indicative bounds on the lifecycle intensity that renewable e-methanol can plausibly attain. The assumed value of 7 gCO2eq/MJ lies within them, and the assessment is repeated at both bounds to test how far the result depends on this assumption.

The 46F burns methanol with a pilot fuel for ignition, since methanol does not autoignite reliably under compression; the pilot is a distillate fuel and supplies about 5% of the energy released. The calculations reported below assume methanol alone, and the effect of the pilot is quantified here. Holding the delivered power and the engine efficiency constant, a 5% pilot share corresponds to 1277 kg/day of marine gas oil together with 52,070 kg/day of methanol, in place of 54,810 kg/day of methanol. Tank-to-wake CO2 rises from 75.4 to 75.7 t/day, a difference of 0.4%, because at the exhaust the two fuels carry almost the same carbon per unit of energy, 69.1 against 75.1 gCO2/MJ.

On a well-to-wake basis, the intensity of the blend is the energy-weighted mean of the two fuels, which gives 11.34 gCO2eq/MJ for the base case and 8.30 and 31.48 gCO2eq/MJ at the two bounds above. All three remain below the Direct Compliance Target throughout 2028–2035, with the least favorable at 21.7 gCO2eq/MJ in 2035, so the pilot fuel does not alter the compliance result. Sulfur oxide emissions are not nil in that case, since the pilot is a distillate fuel: at the same sulfur limit, they amount to 2.6 kg/day, compared with 49.7 kg/day for diesel operation, so the reduction is 95% rather than complete elimination. The tables and figures report the methanol-only case, and the pilot fuel is treated as a sensitivity.

We used a bottom-up methodology to estimate fuel consumption and pollutant emissions. This methodology has been widely used in maritime emission studies because it incorporates both vessel operating characteristics and fuel consumption parameters [7,21,35].

The calculations were conducted for a 24 h sailing period under full operational power demand of 6090 kW.

The Lower Heating Value directly affects the specific fuel consumption (SFC). For a given engine efficiency ( η ), the SFC can be estimated as

S F C = 3.6 η × L H V

(1)

where SFC is the specific fuel consumption (kg/kWh); η is the brake thermal efficiency of the engine (dimensionless); and LHV is the lower heating value of the fuel (MJ/kg), representing the net thermal energy released during the complete combustion of one kilogram of fuel, excluding the latent heat of vaporization of the water produced during combustion. The Lower Heating Value (LHV) varies with each fuel’s chemical composition and directly influences the amount of fuel required to produce a given engine power.

Conventional marine diesel fuels typically have an LHV of 42–43 MJ/kg, whereas methanol has a considerably lower LHV, generally 19–20 MJ/kg. Consequently, methanol contains approximately half the usable energy per unit mass of diesel fuel, resulting in higher specific fuel consumption under identical operating conditions.

The main engine fuel consumption was determined using engine power, specific fuel consumption, and operating time. Total fuel consumption is expressed as

F t r i p = S F C M E × P × t

(2)

where Ftrip is the fuel consumption of the trip, SFCME is the specific fuel consumption of the main engine (g/kWh), P is the power of the main engine in kW, and t is the trip duration in hours.

Carbon dioxide emissions (ECO2) were calculated from fuel consumption and the carbon conversion factor (Cf) of each fuel, making them consistent with specific fuel consumption. The total tank-to-wake carbon dioxide emissions are given by

ECO2 = Ftrip × CfCO2

(3)

where Ftrip is the fuel consumption of the trip, and CfCO2 is the CO2 conversion factor of the fuel (g CO2/g fuel) given in Table 4.

Nitrogen oxide emissions (ENOx) were calculated using the engine power, operating time, and the NOx emission factor according to

ENOx = P × EFNOx × t

(4)

where EFNOx is the NOx emission factor. IMO regulates NOx emissions from marine diesel engines using a tier-based system. The limits are expressed in terms of engine speed n (revolutions per minute, rpm) and are defined in grams of NOx per kilowatt-hour (g/kWh). Equation (5) gives the IMO regulatory limits for 130 ≤ n < 2000 rpm under Tier II and Tier III, which are compared here with the emissions of the two engines at 167 rpm and at 600 rpm, respectively.

NOx = 44⋅n − 0.23 (Tier II); NOx = 9⋅n − 0.20 (Tier III)

(5)

Similarly, sulfur oxide emissions were calculated using the sulfur oxide emission factor as

ESOx = P × EFSOx × t

(6)

where EFSOx is the emission factor of SOx.

Under the Net-Zero Framework, the attained GFI is defined per unit of energy used on board, i.e., per MJ of fuel on a lower calorific value basis (Regulations 2.3.8 and 33.2 of the draft revised Annex VI), not per unit of shaft work [13]. The annual energy used on board is therefore calculated as

E a n n u a l = F a n n u a l × L C V × 10 3

(7)

where Eannual is the annual energy used on board (MJ/year), Fannual is the annual fuel consumption (t/year), given by Equation (8), and LCV is the lower calorific value of the fuel (MJ/kg). The implied brake thermal efficiencies of the two engines at the operating point, 3.6/(SFC × LCV), are 49.6% (diesel) and 48.2% (methanol), which serve as a consistency check of the input data.

Annual GFI analyses were conducted assuming 300 operating days per year under the same conditions. The annual fuel consumption is determined using

F a n n u a l = F d a y × D

(8)

where F a n n u a l is the annual fuel consumption (t/year), F d a y is the daily fuel consumption (t/day), and D is the annual number of operating days, assumed to be 300 in the present study.

The annual fuel cost is calculated as

F C = F a n n u a l × F P

(9)

where F C is the annual fuel cost (USD/year), F a n n u a l is the annual fuel consumption (t/year), and F P is the fuel price (USD/t).

According to the IMO Net-Zero Framework, the reference greenhouse gas fuel intensity is defined as

G F I 2008 = 93.3 g C O 2 e q / M J

(10)

The annual target greenhouse gas fuel intensity is calculated using

G F I T a r g e t = G F I 2008 1 R 100

(11)

where GFITarget is the target greenhouse gas fuel intensity (gCO2eq/MJ), GFI2008 is the IMO reference greenhouse gas fuel intensity based on the 2008 baseline (93.3 gCO2eq/MJ), and R is the applicable annual greenhouse gas reduction target (%). The attained greenhouse gas fuel intensity of each fuel corresponds to its Well-to-Wake (WtW) lifecycle greenhouse gas intensity. The reduction targets are those of Table 4 of Regulation 35 of the draft revised Annex VI [13].

To evaluate compliance with the IMO Net-Zero Framework, the annual Well-to-Wake greenhouse gas emissions are calculated as

C O 2 e q = G F I F u e l × E a n n u a l 10 6

(12)

where C O 2 e q is the annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions (tCO2eq/year), G F I F u e l is the attained greenhouse gas fuel intensity of the evaluated fuel (gCO2eq/MJ), and E a n n u a l is the annual propulsion energy demand (MJ/year). The denominator 10 6 converts grams of carbon dioxide equivalent into metric tonnes.

The annual greenhouse gas emissions corresponding to the IMO Base Target are calculated using

C O 2 e q B a s e = G F I B a s e × E a n n u a l 10 6

(13)

where C O 2 e q B a s e is the allowable annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions associated with the IMO Base Target (tCO2eq/year), and G F I B a s e is the greenhouse gas fuel intensity specified by the IMO Base Target (gCO2eq/MJ).

Similarly, the annual greenhouse gas emissions corresponding to the Direct Compliance Target are determined as

C O 2 e q D i r e c t = G F I D i r e c t × E a n n u a l 10 6

(14)

where C O 2 e q D i r e c t is the allowable annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions corresponding to the IMO Direct Compliance Target (tCO2eq/year), and G F I D i r e c t is the greenhouse gas fuel intensity specified by the Direct Compliance Target (gCO2eq/MJ).

The GFI compliance deficits are determined in accordance with Regulation 36.4 of the draft revised Annex VI [13]. If the attained greenhouse gas fuel intensity exceeds the IMO Base Target, the Tier 1 GFI compliance deficit is determined using

D T 1 = C O 2 e q B a s e − C O 2 e q D i r e c t

(15)

where DT1 is the Tier 1 GFI compliance deficit (tCO2eq/year), CO2eqBase is the allowable annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions under the IMO Base Target (tCO2eq/year), and CO2eqDirect is the allowable annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions under the IMO Direct Compliance Target (tCO2eq/year). If the attained intensity is equal to or below the Base Target but above the Direct Compliance Target, the Tier 1 deficit is instead CO2eqFuel − CO2eqDirect and no Tier 2 deficit arises; if it is equal to or below the Direct Compliance Target, the ship is in direct compliance and receives surplus units equal to CO2eqDirect − CO2eqFuel. The term remedial unit is reserved for the unit acquired from the IMO Net-Zero Fund to balance a deficit (Regulation 2.3.11).

For a ship above the Base Target, the Tier 2 GFI compliance deficit is calculated as

D T 2 = C O 2 e q F u e l − C O 2 e q B a s e

(16)

where DT2 is the Tier 2 GFI compliance deficit (tCO2eq/year), CO2eqFuel is the annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of the evaluated fuel (tCO2eq/year), and CO2eqBase is the allowable annual lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions under the IMO Base Target (tCO2eq/year).

The annual Tier 1 compliance cost is determined by

P e n a l t y T 1 = D T 1 × 100

(17)

where PenaltyT1 is the annual Tier 1 greenhouse gas compliance cost (USD/year), DT1 is the Tier 1 GFI compliance deficit (tCO2eq/year), and 100 represents the IMO Tier 1 remedial unit price (USD/tCO2eq) for the reporting periods 2028 to 2030 (Regulation 36.8).

The annual Tier 2 compliance cost is calculated as

P e n a l t y T 2 = D T 2 × 380

(18)

where PenaltyT2 is the annual Tier 2 greenhouse gas compliance cost (USD/year), DT2 is the Tier 2 GFI compliance deficit (tCO2eq/year), and 380 represents the IMO Tier 2 remedial unit price (USD/tCO2eq) for the reporting periods 2028 to 2030 (Regulation 36.9). Since the draft text leaves the prices for 2031 onwards to be determined by the Committee (Regulation 36.10), they are assumed constant over 2031–2035; this is an explicit assumption of the study.

Finally, the total annual greenhouse gas compliance penalty is obtained from

P e n a l t y T o t a l = P e n a l t y T 1 + P e n a l t y T 2

(19)

where P e n a l t y T o t a l is the total annual greenhouse gas compliance cost (USD/year), representing the sum of the Tier 1 and Tier 2 remedial payments required under the IMO Net-Zero Framework. This total penalty is subsequently incorporated into the annual operating cost assessment of each propulsion alternative.

3. Results

The present investigation highlights the growing need to transition to low- and zero-carbon propulsion systems in the maritime sector, particularly in vessel categories closely linked to global food supply chains, such as livestock carriers. Beyond directly reducing harmful atmospheric pollutants, the study underscores the broader importance of adopting alternative fuels in response to increasingly stringent international regulatory frameworks governing greenhouse gas emissions [36]. In this context, methanol emerges as a particularly promising solution due to its liquid-state handling characteristics, compatibility with modern engine designs, and ability to significantly improve fuel-related emissions performance.

Overall, the results support the view that methanol-fueled engines constitute a practical transitional technology that can bridge the gap between current fossil-based marine propulsion and future sustainable shipping solutions, particularly in sectors where operational demand is expected to grow steadily in the coming decades.

Recent studies show that time-dependent optimization and load-dependent engine models can more realistically represent vessel operation by accounting for varying power demand and off-design performance. However, such approaches generally require detailed operational profiles, engine performance maps, and optimization algorithms. Therefore, this study uses a simplified, steady-state comparative assessment under identical operating conditions to evaluate the environmental and regulatory performance of diesel and e-methanol propulsion systems, maintaining methodological consistency [23,37].

The fuel consumption of both propulsion systems was calculated using Equation (2) based on the engine power requirement of 6090 kW and an operating period of 24 h. The diesel engine consumes approximately 24.85 t of fuel per day, while the methanol engine requires approximately 54.81 t of fuel per day, a ratio of 2.2 that follows directly from the ratio of lower calorific values.

Using Equation (3), the diesel engine emits approximately 79.7 t of CO2 per day and the methanol engine approximately 75.4 t of CO2 per day, a reduction of only 5.4%: the lower carbon content of methanol per unit mass (37.5% against approximately 87% for diesel) is almost entirely offset by the larger mass of fuel burned, so that the exhaust CO2 of the two engines is of the same order. In contrast, operation on methanol results in substantially lower NOx emissions (3 g/kWh), well below the Tier II limit at 600 rpm. This value, however, exceeds the Tier III limit at that speed by 0.5 g/kWh. Since a non-identical replacement engine must meet Tier III in NOx emission control areas where this is possible (Regulation 13.2.2), methanol operation alone does not guarantee Tier III compliance; this is confirmed by the manufacturer, which states that Tier III compliance of the 46F is ensured by a selective catalytic reduction system in both diesel and methanol modes [27]. An SCR unit would therefore be required for trading in NOx emission control areas, with the corresponding space, weight, and reagent-consumption implications for the retrofit. Outside emission control areas, both engines comply with Tier II, the methanol engine with a substantially larger margin.

Sulfur oxide emissions (Equation (6)) fall from 49.7 kg/day for diesel, computed from the 0.10% m/m sulfur limit of Regulation 14, to zero for methanol, which contains no sulfur. The reduction is complete for any fuel sulfur content: at the 0.50% m/m global limit, the diesel figure would be 248.5 kg/day, and the elimination would be correspondingly larger in absolute terms.

The introduction of the IMO Net-Zero Framework represents one of the most significant regulatory changes in maritime decarbonization because it shifts compliance from measuring onboard emissions alone to evaluating the complete lifecycle greenhouse gas intensity of marine fuels.

Unlike previous regulations that primarily targeted exhaust emissions, the Greenhouse GFI framework includes both Well-to-Tank (WtT) and Tank-to-Wake (TtW) emissions, requiring shipowners to consider the environmental impacts of fuel production, transportation, distribution, and onboard combustion. Consequently, the selection of future marine fuels will likely depend more on lifecycle carbon intensity than on engine efficiency or fuel price alone.

The GFI values discussed in the following paragraphs are well-to-wake lifecycle indicators; they are not the exhaust emissions reported above. The present study indicates that e-methanol provides a substantial compliance advantage over conventional marine diesel under the IMO GFI framework. Although methanol has a significantly higher specific fuel consumption because of its lower heating value, its lifecycle greenhouse gas intensity remains considerably lower than that of diesel.

The conventional Wärtsilä W7X35 diesel engine attains a lifecycle greenhouse gas intensity of 93.9 gCO2eq/MJ, above the 2008 reference value, exceeding both annual compliance thresholds from the first year of implementation. The Tier 1 deficit is constant at 3861 tCO2eq/year because it equals the difference between the two targets, which is fixed at 13% of the reference value throughout 2028–2035 (Equation (15)); the Tier 2 deficit grows from 1388 to 9110 tCO2eq/year as the Base Target tightens. Although the excess above the Base Target is relatively small during the initial years, the progressive tightening of the IMO reduction pathway rapidly increases the compliance gap.

This finding illustrates a fundamental characteristic of the GFI framework: a fuel that is only marginally non-compliant today becomes increasingly uneconomical as regulatory targets tighten. Therefore, evaluate compliance not only for the current year but also across the vessel’s entire operational lifetime.

One of the most significant findings of this study is the rapid escalation of compliance costs associated with diesel operation. Because the attained diesel GFI remains constant while the allowable GFI decreases annually, the Tier 2 GFI compliance deficit increases every year, while the Tier 1 deficit remains constant. Consequently, annual compliance costs rise from USD 0.91 million in 2028 to USD 3.85 million in 2035, with the Tier 1 component at USD 0.39 million per year, resulting in cumulative compliance costs of USD 17.7 million over the analyzed period.

This trend indicates that regulatory costs are likely to become a significant component of vessel operating expenditure. 4. Discussion

The economic comparison also demonstrates that fuel price alone is no longer an appropriate indicator for evaluating alternative marine fuels. Conventional diesel has historically maintained an economic advantage because of its relatively low purchase cost and established global supply infrastructure. However, the IMO Net-Zero Framework fundamentally changes this assessment by assigning financial value to lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions.

Consequently, fuels with lower lifecycle carbon intensity, despite higher purchase prices, become progressively more attractive as targets tighten because they avoid greenhouse gas compliance costs. This transition shifts from minimizing fuel expenditure to minimizing total lifecycle operating costs.

The results indicate that methanol consumption is more than twice that of diesel because methanol possesses approximately half the lower heating value of conventional marine fuels. Nevertheless, this increase in fuel consumption does not translate into higher lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions because the carbon intensity of renewable e-methanol is substantially lower, although, as shown above, it does not reduce CO2 emitted at the stack. Consequently, although producing the same propulsion power requires more fuel mass, overall lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions remain significantly below those of diesel.

Another important implication concerns long-term investment decisions for shipowners. Marine propulsion systems typically remain in operation for more than two decades, meaning that engines installed today will continue operating throughout multiple phases of the IMO decarbonization roadmap. Under these conditions, selecting propulsion systems solely based on present-day fuel costs may expose operators to considerable regulatory and financial risks in future years. The analysis indicates that methanol-compatible propulsion systems provide substantially greater resilience to progressively tightening greenhouse gas regulations while reducing uncertainty about future compliance costs.

The environmental benefits observed in this study extend beyond greenhouse gas reduction. The methanol engine reduced nitrogen oxide emissions by more than 73% and eliminated sulfur oxide emissions, while leaving tank-to-wake carbon dioxide emissions almost unchanged. The NOx emissions of the methanol engine remain below the Tier II limit at 600 rpm by a wide margin but above the Tier III limit at that speed, so that an after-treatment system would be required in NOx emission control areas. In comparison, the diesel engine operates 2.4 g/kWh below its Tier II limit. Therefore, methanol contributes simultaneously to climate-change mitigation, on a well-to-wake basis, and improved local air quality.

The findings of the present investigation are consistent with recent studies identifying renewable methanol as one of the most promising transition fuels for international shipping. Du et al. [33] report lifecycle greenhouse gas emission savings of 95.96% for e-methanol produced from offshore wind electricity and captured carbon dioxide, and project that its production cost could reach parity with conventional marine fuels between 2030 and 2035 under the European regulatory framework.

5. Conclusions

This study compared the conventional Wärtsilä W7X35 diesel engine on board the livestock carrier MV Ganado Express with a Wärtsilä 46F methanol-fueled engine at the same propulsion power in a steady-state, 24 h scenario, and assessed compliance with the IMO Net-Zero Framework for 2028–2035 using the target values and definitions of the draft revised MARPOL Annex VI. The main objective was to quantify the environmental and regulatory implications of the replacement while maintaining the vessel’s required propulsion power.

At the exhaust, the methanol engine reduced NOX emissions from 1637 kg/day to 438.5 kg/day, a 73.21% reduction based on the assumed emission factors, and fully removed SOX emissions, which fell from 49.7 kg/day to zero because methanol contains no sulfur. Daily tank-to-wake carbon dioxide emissions, however, decreased only from 79.7 t to 75.4 t, a reduction of 5.4%, because methanol is a carbon-bearing fuel; with the assumed emission factor, the methanol engine also exceeds the Tier III NOx limit at 600 rpm, so an after-treatment system would be required in NOx emission control areas.

The Greenhouse GFI analysis showed that the decarbonization benefit is a well-to-wake effect. Although the diesel engine consumes less fuel, its attained GFI exceeds both the IMO Base Target and the Direct Compliance Target from 2028 onward. As a result, the vessel would face Tier 1 and Tier 2 compliance deficits costing USD 0.91 to 3.85 million per year (USD 17.7 million cumulatively). In contrast, renewable e-methanol reduces annual lifecycle emissions from 29,897 to 2291 tCO2eq and remains below the Direct Compliance Target throughout the 2028–2035 period across the plausible range of e-methanol intensities, from 3.8 to 28.2 gCO2eq/MJ, and therefore avoids greenhouse gas compliance costs.

This shows that lifecycle emissions can be more important than fuel consumption alone when evaluating the long-term economic performance of marine fuels. E-methanol nevertheless remains more expensive in absolute terms at the assumed prices; the annual cost gap narrows from USD 15.1 million to USD 12.2 million by 2035, and its closure depends on post-2035 targets, remedial-unit prices not yet set, and fuel price evolution. The study is also relevant to the livestock shipping sector, where future demand is expected to increase. However, the analysis is limited by its steady-state approach and constant operating assumptions. Future studies should include realistic voyage profiles and changing engine loads.

However, this study is limited to a single livestock carrier and a steady-state, 24 h operating scenario with constant propulsion demand. The analysis relies on published emission factors, fuel prices, and lifecycle GFI values, without modeling transient engine loads, retrofit engineering (gearbox, tank volume, safety systems), methanol storage, bunkering availability, safety implications, operational variability, or the outcome of the pending adoption of the Framework.

Future research should incorporate voyage-specific load profiles, transient engine performance, sensitivity and uncertainty analyses, and full techno-economic lifecycle assessment. Further studies should examine retrofit feasibility, fuel-tank integration, safety and crew requirements, methanol availability, price volatility, renewable-production pathways, and comparisons with ammonia, hydrogen and hybrid propulsion across different livestock-vessel classes.

name: Maritime Transport
title: Advancing sustainable fuels for aviation and maritime industry - Oman Observer
description:
Global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production is expected to reach roughly 2.4 million tonnes this year - less than one percent of all aviation fuel consumed.
The maritime industry, meanwhile, is pursuing wind-assist technologies, efficiency improvements, and dual-fuel vessels, but its transition to sustainable fuels remains problematic.
Behind the crunch lie two linked constraints: limited availability of sustainable feedstocks and biocrudes suitable for refining, and insufficient biorefinery capacity.
Its cultivation can generate biocrude suitable for conversion into high-quality sustainable fuel, alongside biomass that can be used for other productive purposes.
The country stands to benefit substantially from switching to sustainable fuels, particularly as new technologies move towards full cost competitiveness.
text:
Nearly all fuel used today derives from fossil fuels. In reality, for hard-to-abate sectors like aviation, shipping and heavy road transport, there is limited availability of viable sustainable fuel available at the scale required to undertake a meaningful shift. The small pool of biofuel drawing on used cooking oil and tallow is expensive, variable in quality and difficult to access. Unlike passenger and lightweight vehicles - which can take advantage of advancing battery technology - aircraft and vessels carrying heavy payloads across oceans cannot, and will continue to require the energy density that liquid fuels provide.

The constraint at hand carries severe consequences. Global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production is expected to reach roughly 2.4 million tonnes this year - less than one percent of all aviation fuel consumed. The maritime industry, meanwhile, is pursuing wind-assist technologies, efficiency improvements, and dual-fuel vessels, but its transition to sustainable fuels remains problematic. Reaching net-zero by 2050 will require annual SAF output in the vicinity of 500 million tonnes - a more than 200-fold expansion within 24 years. Behind the crunch lie two linked constraints: limited availability of sustainable feedstocks and biocrudes suitable for refining, and insufficient biorefinery capacity. Refiners are, understandably, reluctant to commit capital without assurance of consistent feedstock supply.

While bio-based fuels already exist, their supply base is limited and, in certain respects, contentious. Crop-derived feedstocks - including corn, soy and palm - compete directly with food production and can drive land conversion, including the expansion of large-scale monocultures at the expense of natural ecosystems and, in some cases, primary forest. Used cooking oil and animal tallow belong to the more defensible alternatives, but their available supply is inherently limited and increasingly sought after. The dominant SAF production pathway today relies heavily on these and other lipid feedstocks, making diversification increasingly important. Under EU regulation, this constraint is reflected in policy: waste oils and fats sit in Annex IX, Part B of the Renewable Energy Directive and are capped at 1.7% of the transport fuel mix. Advanced feedstocks such as forestry residues, other lignocellulosic materials and algae can mitigate many of these pressures.

With freshwater already scarce and limited national land suitable for agriculture, balancing food security, energy security, and decarbonisation poses a formidable challenge for countries like Oman. Absent a domestic feedstock, Oman's alternative is longer term reliance on imported fuel, or imported feedstock for domestic refining.

Oman does possess, however, several thousand kilometres of pristine coastline, among the highest levels of solar irradiance globally, and extensive desert land with no competing agricultural value. These conditions offer a strong match for a newly identified marine microalga – Sphaerica - a feedstock with potentially high commercial as well as environmental value. Its cultivation can generate biocrude suitable for conversion into high-quality sustainable fuel, alongside biomass that can be used for other productive purposes.

This particular organism needs no freshwater but thrives in very high salinity seawater, and the water drawn into the system can be recycled through multiple cycles rather than extracted once and then discarded - a meaningful distinction for a country that already directs much of its scarce freshwater to agriculture.

Nor does it require arable soil. Cultivation takes place on land with no food-producing value, leaving soil health undisturbed, within an enclosed photobioreactor system designed not to degrade the land beneath it and using lightweight, modular construction. Genuine diversification means directing future investment towards feedstocks that can grow at scale and achieve acceptable cost structures without reproducing the sustainability problems associated with earlier generations of biofuels. Oman's coastline and sunlight give it the means to lead that shift.

I’m presently visiting the country, leading a delegation from a UK biotechnology company, HutanBio, which is dedicated to innovation in this respect. Taking part in the Oman Climate Week we benefit from conversation with multiple parties, exploring ways our bioenergy platform can be taken forward in Oman, thereby scaling production of a sustainable, quality bio/fuel, to serve Oman as well as international markets.

Oman – along with the wider region – continues to evolve as a vibrant hub for air passengers, air cargo, and maritime transport. The country stands to benefit substantially from switching to sustainable fuels, particularly as new technologies move towards full cost competitiveness. By pushing ahead with the bio-energy opportunities now taking shape, Oman has an opportunity to become a significant producer - and ultimately exporter - of sustainable fuels, produced domestically using resources the country has in abundance rather than those it must import. A rising fuel bill can thus be turned into the foundation for a new export industry, helping to diversify revenue as Vision 2040 intends rather than trading one import dependency for another.

Dominic Emery

The writer is Chair of HutanBio and a veteran expert in climate change and the energy transition.

title: NORRÖNA saves up to 26 tonnes of CO2 per week using shore power in Iceland | Shippax
description:
The shore-power project was carried out in cooperation with the local municipality of Múlaþing, which was responsible for the shoreside work.
Faroese company ETV designed and installed the shore-power solution aboard NORRÖNA.
Shore power allows NORRÖNA to shut down its auxiliary engines while alongside.
Due to the vessel’s long port stay in Seyðisfjörður, this is estimated to save seven to eight tonnes of fuel per week, corresponding to a reduction in CO2 emissions of approximately 22–26 tonnes per week.
NORRÖNA sails one of the world's longest ferry routes, connecting the Faroe Islands, Denmark, and Iceland.
text:
The shore-power project was carried out in cooperation with the local municipality of Múlaþing, which was responsible for the shoreside work. Faroese company ETV designed and installed the shore-power solution aboard NORRÖNA.

Shore power allows NORRÖNA to shut down its auxiliary engines while alongside. Due to the vessel’s long port stay in Seyðisfjörður, this is estimated to save seven to eight tonnes of fuel per week, corresponding to a reduction in CO2 emissions of approximately 22–26 tonnes per week.

Air and noise pollution are also significantly reduced, as engine noise, vibrations and certain emissions are eliminated when the auxiliary engines are shut down. This improves conditions both on board and for people living and working near the port.

“The project demonstrates what can be achieved when public authorities, ports, shipping companies and suppliers work together on practical solutions. We at Smyril Line are very grateful for the excellent cooperation with the municipality of Múlaþing and ETV,” said Jens Meinhard Rasmussen, CEO of Smyril Line.

Shore power forms part of Smyril Line’s efforts to reduce the environmental impact of its operations and develop sustainable maritime transport in the North Atlantic. Virtually all electricity in Iceland is produced using renewable energy sources - primarily hydroelectric and geothermal energy.

NORRÖNA sails one of the world's longest ferry routes, connecting the Faroe Islands, Denmark, and Iceland.

title: Shipping decarbonisation hinges on fuel costs and delayed IMO rules - Streamline Feed
description:
Fuels that can replace oil at sea Ships cannot plug into a cleaner grid, so decarbonisation depends on new fuels.
Ammonia and methanol can both be made from hydrogen produced by electrolysing water with renewable electricity, then further chemical processing.
The cost gap that stalls investment Before the oil market turbulence linked to the Iran war, green ammonia priced around $600 to $1,050 per tonne against $500 to $600 for heavy fuel oil, the FT reports.
It signed an agreement last year to supply Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH's new dual-fuelled ships.
What would change the calculus Carbon pricing or mandates that close the gap between green ammonia and heavy fuel oil.
text:
Global shipping moves three-quarters of world trade on about 7,000 vessels, the largest of which sail the equivalent of ten return trips to the Moon in their lifetimes, yet the fleet remains almost entirely fossil-fuelled and accounts for about 3 per cent of annual greenhouse gas emissions, with container ships often burning particularly dirty bunker fuel, the FT reported on September 15, 2026.

Fuels that can replace oil at sea

Ships cannot plug into a cleaner grid, so decarbonisation depends on new fuels. Ammonia and methanol can both be made from hydrogen produced by electrolysing water with renewable electricity, then further chemical processing. Their energy densities are similar to fossil fuels, so they can run in existing engines with "little or no" modification and travel through mostly existing infrastructure, according to the Royal Society, the UK science academy.

The cost gap that stalls investment

Before the oil market turbulence linked to the Iran war, green ammonia priced around $600 to $1,050 per tonne against $500 to $600 for heavy fuel oil, the FT reports. Prices in long-term offtake agreements can be significantly lower but are not public, and energy companies have not wanted, or been sufficiently incentivised, to make the necessary investments. David Fishman, an energy analyst at the Lantau Group in Shanghai, told the FT that scale and experience, not new chemistry, will drive costs down: "We're not innovating a new chemical process here."

Regulation is the other lever. Penalties and minimum carbon prices on fossil fuel use would kick-start demand, the FT notes, and a 2025 report commissioned by the UK transport department found that stronger policy support for sustainable fuels could cut shipping emissions by 95 per cent, with green ammonia the lowest-cost pathway.

Emissions keep rising

Efficiency gains have not bent the curve. Total "tank-to-wake" emissions from fuel use onboard rose 12 per cent between 2016 and 2023 because trade growth outpaced them, and black carbon emissions are rising rapidly, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation. Shipowners have long touted efficiency improvements as evidence of climate commitment, but the data show incremental gains inside fossil-fuelled engines losing to trade expansion.

China pulls ahead while IMO talks stall

Mission Possible Partnership data cited by the FT show 12 ammonia production sites in China have passed final funding approval and 54 more are announced, alongside 21 methanol plants approved and 88 announced. Some $23.7bn has been invested across the 33 Chinese methanol and ammonia projects that are operational or have reached final investment decision; comparative figures are not available for Europe or the US.

State-owned CEEC claims its Jilin facility, in China's far north-east, is the world's largest of its kind, producing 45,000 tonnes of green hydrogen and 200,000 tonnes of green ammonia and methanol a year. It signed an agreement last year to supply Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH's new dual-fuelled ships. China's latest five-year plan names green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol as core pillars of non-electricity renewable use, prompting initiatives from listed companies Envision and Towngas, state shipping giant COSCO and Shanghai International Port Group.

The multilateral counterweight has stalled. An International Maritime Organization effort to agree a climate deal for shipping, which the FT notes could have encouraged other countries to compete with China in clean fuels, was adjourned in October 2025 amid US and Saudi Arabian opposition. The IMO confirms its Marine Environment Protection Committee adjourned the extraordinary session on the Net-Zero Framework for one year, to reconvene in October 2026, with an intersessional working group continuing work on implementation guidelines in the meantime.

What would change the calculus

Carbon pricing or mandates that close the gap between green ammonia and heavy fuel oil.

Scale and operating experience in electrolysers and synthesis, per Lantau's Fishman.

Policy certainty from the IMO session reconvening in October 2026.

Clean fuel project pipeline by region, Mission Possible Partnership data cited by the FTRegionAmmonia sites approved / announcedMethanol plants approved / announcedInvestment notedChina12 / 5421 / 88$23.7bn across 33 projects operational or at FIDEurope1 clean ammonia projectNot reportedNo comparable figuresUS5 clean ammonia projectsNot reportedNo comparable figures

Until then, the industry's clean-fuel geography is being set by Chinese state support and Chinese renewable capacity, while Europe and the US wait on a rulebook that slips a year at a time and on fuels the FT describes as key to reducing vessels' large greenhouse gas emissions.

name: Biofuels & Shipping
title: Marine biofuels deployable near term, but feedstock availability constrains growth
description:
Marine biofuels are emerging as a readily deployable near-term decarbonization option for the shipping sector, although tightening feedstock availability constrains growth as demand scales, industry participants told Platts at APPEC 2026 in Singapore.
“B24, B30, they’re definitely scalable; however…not indefinitely,” Chris Chatterton, maritime director at the Global Center for Green Fuels, said at a separate low-carbon marine fuels panel.
Feedstock supply is therefore becoming a key consideration in determining whether projects can secure financing and move toward commercial scale.
Near-term prospects for biofuels come amid longer commercialization timelines expected for some other low-carbon marine fuels.
Despite biofuels’ near-term advantage, shipping is unlikely to converge on a single replacement fuel.
text:
Marine biofuels are emerging as a readily deployable near-term decarbonization option for the shipping sector, although tightening feedstock availability constrains growth as demand scales, industry participants told Platts at APPEC 2026 in Singapore.

Biofuels are the “lowest hanging fruit” among lower-carbon marine fuels because they are relatively easy to blend and incorporate into existing engines, Nathanael Lin, partner for shipping and international trade at Rajah & Tann Singapore, said at a shipping panel Sept. 10.

The sector can also draw on broadly similar storage infrastructure for conventional fuels, as well as on financiers and underwriters already familiar with the products, reducing barriers to adoption, Lin said.

The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore data shows that biobunker sales in the world’s largest bunkering hub retreated to around 39,000 mt in July, accounting for less than 1% of the total bunker sales in the month, compared to 135,000 mt in the same month the previous year. For the first seven months of 2026, total biobunker sales stood at 457,000 mt, down from 907,900 mt in the same period the previous year.

Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed Singapore-delivered B24 low-sulfur biobunker premiums at $232/mt over the Platts FOB Singapore Marine Fuel 0.5%S cargo assessment Sept. 10, down $2/mt week over week. Singapore-delivered B30 low-sulfur biobunker premiums fell $3/mt over the same period to $267/mt.

In the high-sulfur segment, Singapore-delivered B24 high-sulfur biobunker premiums were assessed at $244/mt over the Platts FOB Singapore 380 CST 3.5%S fuel oil cargo assessment, down $6/mt week over week. B30 high-sulfur bio-bunker premiums were assessed at $293/mt, down $9/mt over the same period.

Shipowners are already expanding their use following trials.

NYK Line’s biodiesel consumption increased by “more than 40 times or even 50 times” from 2023 levels after the Japanese shipowner completed a six-month B24 trial under Project LOTUS with the Global Center for Maritime Decarbonization, according to Ryogo Nakajima, decarbonization promotion team lead at NYK.

The trial found no issues with longer-term B24 use under the tested conditions, Nakajima said. NYK is now undertaking an almost year-long B100 trial to assess the effects of higher-purity biodiesel on its vessels and engines.

However, greater adoption is putting the availability and aggregation of sustainable feedstocks increasingly in focus.

“B24, B30, they’re definitely scalable; however…not indefinitely,” Chris Chatterton, maritime director at the Global Center for Green Fuels, said at a separate low-carbon marine fuels panel.

Rather than focusing solely on increasing blend ratios, the industry needs to broaden the pool of available feedstocks to support further growth, Chatterton said.

Feedstock constraints are also emerging as a hurdle to financing new biofuel projects.

“The aggregation is a problem,” said Karthik Sathiavageeswaran, executive director for energy, renewables, and infrastructure at DBS Bank.

While technology risks for many projects are increasingly manageable, some developers seeking capital “really can’t demonstrate sustainable feedstock that comes in,” he said. Feedstock supply is therefore becoming a key consideration in determining whether projects can secure financing and move toward commercial scale.

Near-term prospects for biofuels come amid longer commercialization timelines expected for some other low-carbon marine fuels. Juwita Setiawan, trading manager at Sing Fuels, said she expected biofuels and LNG to lead alternative marine fuels in the near term, followed by methanol in the medium term, while synthetic fuels could become more important as emissions targets tighten toward 2040 and beyond.

S&P Global Energy expects the traditional bunker fuels’ share will decline from 85% in 2030 to 26% in 2060 globally on an energy basis, where bio-blends will be used to help vessels comply with tightening EEXI regulations, and their adoption is increasing due to the drop-in nature, typically up to 30%, according to the alternative bunker fuel long-term outlook released Aug. 25. The share of alternative bunker fuels is expected to reach 30% of the fuel mix by 2060, while methanol leads in the short-term and ammonia takes highest market share of 22% by 2060.

Despite biofuels’ near-term advantage, shipping is unlikely to converge on a single replacement fuel. Chatterton said, “Optionality is very high on the agenda for bankability,” as shipowners seek greater flexibility across multiple fuel pathways.
